Cluster scattering diagrams via quiver moduli and tight gradings

Amanda Burcroff Address: Amanda Burcroff, Department of Mathematics, MIT, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email address: amandabu@mit.edu , Kyungyong Lee Address: Kyungyong Lee, Department of Mathematics, University of Alabama, Tuscaloosa, AL 35487, USA and Korea Institute for Advanced Study, Seoul 02455, Republic of Korea Email address: kyungyong.lee@ua.edu & klee1@kias.re.kr , Lang Mou Address: Lang Mou, Department of Mathematics, University of California Davis, One Shields Avenue, Davis, CA 95616, USA Email address: lmou.math@gmail.com , Gregg Musiker Address: Gregg Musiker, School of Mathematics, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN 55455, USA Email address: musiker@umn.edu and Markus Reineke Address: Markus Reineke, Faculty of Mathematics, Ruhr-Universität Bochum, Universitätsstraße 150, 44780 Bochum, Germany Email address: markus.reineke@ruhr-uni-bochum.de
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study rank-2 cluster scattering diagrams through moduli spaces of quiver representations and a recently developed combinatorial framework of tight gradings. Combining quiver-theoretic and combinatorial methods, we prove and extend a collection of conjectures posed by Elgin–Reading–Stella concerning the structural and enumerative properties of the wall-function coefficients. The tight grading perspective also provides a new proof of the Weyl group symmetry of the scattering diagram.

Key words and phrases: 
scattering diagram, quiver moduli, tight grading, cluster algebra, Weyl symmetry

1. Introduction

1.1. Background and motivation

Scattering diagrams [16, 14] are combinatorial structures encoding wall-crossing phenomena arising in various sources of mathematics. Cluster scattering diagrams of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich [11] are a special class attached to cluster algebras/varieties [9, 8], where the wall-functions reflect their mutation structure and positivity properties. In rank 2, they are closely related to the tropical vertex of Gross–Pandharipande–Siebert, where the wall-functions are expressed through generating series of relative Gromov-Witten invariants of toric surfaces [13] and Euler characteristics of quiver moduli [22, 23].

From the cluster algebra perspective, the coefficients of rank-2 wall-functions lead to the Laurent positivity in rank-2 cluster algebras 𝒜⁡(b,c)\mathcal{A}(b,c) of Fomin–Zelevinsky [27]. This positivity admits both combinatorial descriptions via compatible gradings using edges in Dyck paths [18, 17] and more geometric ones via scattering diagrams [11, 15].

Based on extensive computational evidence, Elgin, Reading, and Stella [7] formulated a collection of conjectures regarding the wall-function coefficients τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) of the cluster scattering diagram 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)} associated with 𝒜⁡(b,c)\mathcal{A}(b,c). These conjectures, which primarily concern the dependence of τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) on the positive integers bb and cc, form the starting point of the present work. Tight gradings, recently introduced in [4, 5], refine the framework of compatible gradings [17, 24], and provide a unified combinatorial model for these coefficients. Our approach uses both quiver representation techniques and the combinatorics of tight gradings to confirm many of these predictions and to derive further generalizations.

1.2. Elgin–Reading–Stella’s conjectures

For coprime positive integers dd and ee, write the wall-function on the ray ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec) in the cluster scattering diagram 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)} as the power series

𝔣ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)=1+∑τ⁡(i,j)​x1i​b​x2j​c,\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec)}=1+\sum\tau(i,j)x_{1}^{ib}x_{2}^{jc},

where the sum is over positive integers ii and jj such that (i,j)=(k​d,k​e)(i,j)=(kd,ke) for some k≥1k\geq 1. Note that in the case that (d​b,e​c)(db,ec) is not a primitive vector, we can re-express ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)=ℝ≤0​(v1,v2)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec)=\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2}) for gcd⁡(v1,v2)=1\gcd(v_{1},v_{2})=1. See (2.2) for how these τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) are precisely defined.

Elgin, Reading, and Stella posed the following conjectures and problem.

Conjectures ([7, Conjecture 1–18]).

Let g=gcd⁡(i​b,j​c)/gcd⁡(i,j)g=\gcd(ib,jc)/\gcd(i,j).

    For i,j>0i,j>0, the coefficient τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) is a polynomial in bb, cc, and gg.

1.3. Main results

The above conjectures regard the cluster scattering diagram 𝔇(b,c)=𝔇⁡(1+x1b,1+x2c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)}=\mathfrak{D}(1+x_{1}^{b},1+x_{2}^{c}), which is closely tied with another scattering diagram 𝔇(c,b)∘=𝔇⁡((1+x1)c,(1+x2)b)\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}_{(c,b)}=\mathfrak{D}((1+x_{1})^{c},(1+x_{2})^{b}) via the change-of-lattice transformation; see Section 2. (Beware the swap between bb and cc.)

Let dd and ee be positive integers with gcd⁡(d,e)=1\gcd(d,e)=1. The wall-function of 𝔇(c,b)∘\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}_{(c,b)} on the wall ℝ≤0​(d,e)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e) is written as

𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)∘=1+∑k≥1ϱ⁡(k​d,k​e)​x1k​d​x2k​e.\mathfrak{f}^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\varrho(kd,ke)x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}.

With dd and ee fixed, write τk=τ⁡(k​d,k​e)\tau_{k}=\tau(kd,ke) and ϱk=ϱ⁡(k​d,k​e)\varrho_{k}=\varrho(kd,ke). We summarize in the theorem below the structural properties obtained for τk\tau_{k} and ϱk\varrho_{k}. The proof will be provided in Section 6.

Theorem 1.2.
  1. (1)

    and ϱk\varrho_{k} has a leading term ck​d​bk​ec^{kd}b^{ke} with positive coefficient.

Both λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) and τk\tau_{k} admit enumerative interpretations in terms of tight gradings; see Section 4 for a detailed treatment. Tight gradings were introduced in [4, 5] to give a combinatorial interpretation of rank-22 scattering diagram coefficients. Each tight grading is assignment of nonnegative integer weights to the edges of a Dyck path satisfying certain conditions (see Definition 4.8). They form a subset of the compatible gradings defined by Lee–Li–Zelevinsky [17] (and extended by Rupel [24]) to study the greedy bases of (generalized) cluster algebras. The conditions under which a compatible grading is tight are directly motivated by rank-22 cluster scattering diagrams. Thus tight gradings serve as a bridge between the Lee–Schiffler proof of Laurent positivity using Dyck path combinatorics [19] and the Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich proof via scattering diagrams [11].

The interpretation of λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) and τk\tau_{k} using tight gradings plays an important role in our analysis in Section 6. In Section 5, we give a new description of tight gradings as arrangements of rectangular tiles, called footprints. A similar tiling interpretation was outlined in [5], but the footprint framework admits more tiles and we believe better captures the relative “tightness” of tight gradings.

Quiver moduli are algebraic varieties parametrizing isomorphism classes of stable representations of quivers. Despite being interesting in their own right for encoding hard representation-theoretic classification problems, it turned out that their topological invariants encode enumerative invariants such as Gromov-Witten and Donaldson-Thomas invariants. A typical example is the refined GW/Kronecker correspondence [23]: both types of geometric invariants are encoded in the so-called tropical vertex, now called a rank 22 (generalized) cluster scattering diagram (see the following Section 2). This allows us to translate the above conjectures into statements on Euler characteristics of quiver moduli spaces, and to readily apply results obtained in [23] (in fact, we will therefore never need the precise definition of (stable) quiver representations and their moduli spaces). This method is particularly helpful in obtaining closed formulas for τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j), as in C5 through C10. In particular, Conjectures C7 and C8 above are equivalent to a conjecture of Gross and Pandharipande [12, Conjecture (1,4)], proved in [23, Theorem 9.4].

The next theorem lists the subset of conjectures of Elgin–Reading–Stella that we are able to prove combining the aforementioned techniques.

Theorem 1.4.

C1, C2, C3, C5-C10, C14-C18 are true.

Remark 1.5.

Ryota Akagi [2] has recently given proofs of C1, C2, C3, C5, C6, C15 and obtained partial results on C14, C16, C17, C18. His method is different from ours and builds on his earlier work [1] on dilogarithm identities. He further proves C11 [2, Proposition 4.3], which our method does not address.

Note that Conjectures C4, C12, and C13 remain unsolved. In fact, the conjectural formula C13 is mysterious from both the quiver moduli and tight grading points of view.

Finally, we give an answer to Problem 1.1, using the Lee–Li–Zelevinsky mutation operation on gradings [17] and a retraction operation, both discussed in Section 7.

Theorem 1.6.

The composition of mutation and retraction on tight gradings is a bijection exhibiting the Weyl group symmetry, namely that

τ⁡(i,j)=τ⁡(i,b​i−j)​ and ​τ​(i,j)=τ⁡(c​j−i,j).\tau(i,j)=\tau(i,bi-j)\text{ and }\tau(i,j)=\tau(cj-i,j)\,.

A consequence of Theorem 1.6 is a new combinatorial proof of the invariant structure of 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)} described in [11, Example 1.15]. Note that the proof of the interpretation of τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) in terms of tight gradings in [5, Section 5.5] does not rely on this invariant structure.

2. Rank 2 scattering diagrams and the change-of-lattice

We briefly recall some basics of rank-2 (generalized) cluster scattering diagrams.

Fix a base field 𝕜\Bbbk of characteristic zero. For i=1,2i=1,2, take power series

Pi​(xi)=1+∑k≥1pi,k​xik∈𝕜⁡⟦xi⟧wherepi,k∈𝕜.P_{i}(x_{i})=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{i,k}x_{i}^{k}\in\Bbbk\llbracket x_{i}\rrbracket\quad\text{where}\quad p_{i,k}\in\Bbbk.

By a result of Kontsevich–Soibelman [16], the two power series P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} uniquely determine a consistent scattering diagram

(2.1) 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)={(ℝ⁡(1,0),P1),(ℝ⁡(0,1),P2)}∪{(ℝ≤0(v1,v2),𝔣ℝ≤0​(v1,v2))∣(v1,v2)∈ℤ>02,gcd(v1,v2)=1}.\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2})=\{(\mathbb{R}(1,0),P_{1}),(\mathbb{R}(0,1),P_{2})\}\\ \cup\{(\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2}),\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2})})\mid(v_{1},v_{2})\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2},\gcd(v_{1},v_{2})=1\}.

Every element in 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}), referred to as a wall, is a pair (𝔡,𝔣)(\mathfrak{d},\mathfrak{f}) where 𝔡\mathfrak{d} is either a line or a ray in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} and 𝔣\mathfrak{f} (the wall-function), when 𝔣=𝔣ℝ≤0​(v1,v2)\mathfrak{f}=\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2})}, is a power series in 𝕜⁡⟦x1v1​x2v2⟧\Bbbk\llbracket x_{1}^{v_{1}}x_{2}^{v_{2}}\rrbracket with constant term 11. We refer the reader to [13, Section 1.3] for the algebraic details of the consistency of scattering diagrams and to [4, Section 4.1] for a presentation closer to the current setup.

The primary focus of this paper is the case where

P1​(x1)=1+x1bandP2​(x2)=1+x2cP_{1}(x_{1})=1+x_{1}^{b}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{2}(x_{2})=1+x_{2}^{c}

for positive integers bb and cc. We denote this scattering diagram by 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)}. They are known as the rank-2 special class of the cluster scattering diagrams of Gross–Hacking–Keel–Kontsevich [11], and are closely tied with Fomin–Zelevinsky’s cluster algebras 𝒜⁡(b,c)\mathcal{A}(b,c) in rank 2 [27].

For 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)}, it is also known that each 𝔣ℝ≤0​(v1,v2)\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2})} lives in 𝕜⁡⟦x1d​b​x2e​c⟧\Bbbk\llbracket x_{1}^{db}x_{2}^{ec}\rrbracket for the unique pair

(d,e)∈ℤ>02such thatgcd⁡(d,e)=1andv1​e​c=v2​d​b.(d,e)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}\quad\text{such that}\quad\gcd(d,e)=1\quad\text{and}\quad v_{1}ec=v_{2}db.

Therefore we can write

(2.2) 𝔣ℝ≤0​(v1,v2)=1+∑k≥1τ(b,c)​(k​d,k​e)​x1k​d​b​x2k​e​c,\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(v_{1},v_{2})}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau^{(b,c)}(kd,ke)x_{1}^{kdb}x_{2}^{kec},

defining the coefficients τ⁡(k​d,k​e)=τ(b,c)​(k​d,k​e)\tau(kd,ke)=\tau^{(b,c)}(kd,ke), viewed as functions of bb and cc.

Example 2.3.

Let b=2b=2 and c=3c=3.

If (v1,v2)=(1,1),(v_{1},v_{2})=(1,1), then (d,e)=(3,2)(d,e)=(3,2) and

𝔣ℝ≤0​(1,1)=1+τ⁡(3,2)​x16​x26+τ⁡(6,4)​x112​x212+⋯.\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,1)}=1+\tau(3,2)x_{1}^{6}x_{2}^{6}+\tau(6,4)x_{1}^{12}x_{2}^{12}+\cdots.

On the other hand, if (v1,v2)=(2,3),(v_{1},v_{2})=(2,3), then (d,e)=(1,1)(d,e)=(1,1), and

𝔣ℝ≤0​(2,3)=1+τ⁡(1,1)​x12​x23+τ⁡(2,2)​x14​x26+⋯.\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(2,3)}=1+\tau(1,1)x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{3}+\tau(2,2)x_{1}^{4}x_{2}^{6}+\cdots.

As another example, if (v1,v2)=(3,5),(v_{1},v_{2})=(3,5), then (d,e)=(9,10)(d,e)=(9,10), and

𝔣ℝ≤0​(3,5)=1+τ⁡(9,10)​x118​x230+τ⁡(18,20)​x136​x260+⋯.\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(3,5)}=1+\tau(9,10)x_{1}^{18}x_{2}^{30}+\tau(18,20)x_{1}^{36}x_{2}^{60}+\cdots.

A closely related scattering diagram is

𝔇(c,b)∘≔𝔇⁡((1+x1)c,(1+x2)b).\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}_{(c,b)}\coloneqq\mathfrak{D}((1+x_{1})^{c},(1+x_{2})^{b}).

(Notice the swap between bb and cc.) For positive dd and ee with gcd⁡(d,e)=1\gcd(d,e)=1, denote the wall-function on ℝ≤0​(d,e)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e) by

(2.4) 𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)∘=1+∑k≥1ϱ(c,b)​(k​d,k​e)​x1k​d​x2k​e∈𝕜⁡⟦x1d​x2e⟧,\mathfrak{f}^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\varrho^{(c,b)}(kd,ke)x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}\in\Bbbk\llbracket x_{1}^{d}x_{2}^{e}\rrbracket,

defining the coefficients ϱ⁡(k​d,k​e)=ϱ(c,b)​(k​d,k​e)\varrho(kd,ke)=\varrho^{(c,b)}(kd,ke), viewed as functions of cc and bb.

As pointed out in [11, Example 1.15] (and stated in Proposition 2.5), the scattering diagram 𝔇(c,b)∘\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}_{(c,b)} can be transformed into 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)} by the change-of-lattice trick, given in [11, Proof of Proposition C.13, Step IV]. A more detailed proof of Proposition 2.5 can be found in [10, Proposition 1.12].

Proposition 2.5 (Change-of-lattice).

For each (d,e)∈ℤ>02(d,e)\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{2}, define

g=g⁡(d,e,b,c)≔gcd⁡(d​b,e​c)/gcd⁡(d,e).g=g(d,e,b,c)\coloneqq\gcd(db,ec)/\gcd(d,e).

Then we have for gcd⁡(d,e)=1\gcd(d,e)=1,

𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)∘=(1+∑k≥1τ⁡(k​d,k​e)​x1k​d​x2k​e)b​c/g.\mathfrak{f}^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)}=\left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau(kd,ke)x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}\right)^{bc/g}.

This is an important tool that we use throughout the paper, especially in Sections 3 and 6.

3. Wall-functions via quiver moduli

In this section, we prove C1, C5, C6, C7, C8, C9, and C10 by the quiver method.

Namely, Proposition 2.5 allows us to translate between the notation and conventions of [7] and of [23]. We define S(d,e)​(t)S_{(d,e)}(t) by

S(d,e)​(t)=∑k≥0τ⁡(k​d,k​e)​tk∈ℚ⁡⟦t⟧S_{(d,e)}(t)=\sum_{k\geq 0}\tau(kd,ke)t^{k}\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket t\rrbracket

and readily find

Corollary 3.1.

We have

S(d,e)​(t)=f(d,e)​(t)g/b​c.S_{(d,e)}(t)=f_{(d,e)}(t)^{g/bc}.
Proof.

Set l1=bl_{1}=b, l2=cl_{2}=c , and consider the series f(d,e)​(t)∈ℚ⁡⟦t⟧f_{(d,e)}(t)\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket t\rrbracket appearing in the tropical vertex factorization [23, Section 2, (1)], where we specialize all sks_{k} and all tlt_{l} to tt, and specialize xx and yy to 11. Then f(d,e)​(t)=𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)∘|x1d​x2e=tf_{(d,e)}(t)=\mathfrak{f}^{\circ}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)}|_{x_{1}^{d}x_{2}^{e}=t} while S(d,e)​(t)=𝔣ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)|x1d​b​x2e​c=tS_{(d,e)}(t)=\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec)}|_{x_{1}^{db}x_{2}^{ec}=t}. Proposition 2.5 implies the desired identity. ∎

For the details of the following notions, we refer to [23] (in fact, as mentioned earlier, we do not need these notions in detail here). We consider the complete bipartite quiver K⁡(b,c)K(b,c) with arrows from a set of cc vertices to a set of bb vertices. Given a dimension vector (ℙ1,ℙ2)(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2}) with ℙ1=(p1,1,…,p1,b)\mathbb{P}_{1}=(p_{1,1},\ldots,p_{1,b}), ℙ2=(p2,1,…,p2,c)\mathbb{P}_{2}=(p_{2,1},\ldots,p_{2,c}) for K⁡(b,c)K(b,c), let Mst​(ℙ1,ℙ2)M^{\rm st}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2}) be the moduli space parametrizing isomorphism classes of stable representations of K⁡(b,c)K(b,c) of dimension vector (ℙ1,ℙ2)(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2}) with respect to the non-trivial symmetric stability, and define the following sum of topological Euler characteristics:

χ(d,e)​(k)=∑χ⁡(Mst​(ℙ1,ℙ2)),\chi_{(d,e)}(k)=\sum\chi(M^{\rm st}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2})),

the sum ranging over all ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} summing up to k​dkd, and all ℙ2\mathbb{P}_{2} summing up to k​eke.

Then [23, Theorem 8.1] immediately implies that the series f(d,e)​(t)f_{(d,e)}(t) is determined by a functional equation:

Theorem 3.2.

The series f(d,e)​(t)∈ℚ⁡⟦t⟧f_{(d,e)}(t)\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket t\rrbracket is determined by

f(d,e)​(t)=∏k≥1(1−(t​f(d,e)​(t)E)k)−k​χ(d,e)​(k),f_{(d,e)}(t)=\prod_{k\geq 1}(1-(tf_{(d,e)}(t)^{E})^{k})^{-k\chi_{(d,e)}(k)},

where E=(b​c​d​e−b​d2−c​e2)/b​cE=(bcde-bd^{2}-ce^{2})/bc.

Combining the previous results, we note:

Corollary 3.3.

S(d,e)​(t)S_{(d,e)}(t) is determined by the functional equation

S(d,e)(t)=∏k≥1(1−(tS(d,e)(t)b​c​E/g)k)−kχ(d,e)(k)g/bc.S_{(d,e)}(t)=\prod_{k\geq 1}(1-(tS_{(d,e)}(t)^{bcE/g})^{k})^{-k\chi_{(d,e)}(k)g/bc}.
Proof.

This immediately follows from Corollary 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. ∎

We will use this characterization below to prove C1. But first we prove C5–C10.

We consider the t1t^{1}-coefficients of S(d,e)​(t)S_{(d,e)}(t) and f(d,e)​(t)f_{(d,e)}(t) to find, using [23, Corollary 9.1]:

If ii and jj are coprime, we have

τ⁡(i,j)=gb​c​χ(i,j)​(1).\tau(i,j)=\frac{g}{bc}\chi_{(i,j)}(1).

In particular, [23, Theorem 9.4] already solves C9 and C10.

Proposition 3.4 ([23, Theorem 9.4]).

We have

τ⁡(i,i−1)=gi⁡((b−1)​i+1)​((b−1)​(c−1)​i+c−1i−1),\displaystyle\tau(i,i-1)=\frac{g}{i((b-1)i+1)}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i+c-1}{i-1},
τ⁡(j−1,j)=gj⁡(j​c−j+1)​((j​c−j+1)​(b−1)j−1).\displaystyle\tau(j-1,j)=\frac{g}{j(jc-j+1)}\binom{(jc-j+1)(b-1)}{j-1}.

Regarding C5 and C6, we give two proofs. The first proof is given below, and the second proof follows from the more general formula in Proposition 8.1.

Proposition 3.5.

We have

τ⁡(1,j)=gb​(bj)andτ⁡(i,1)=gc​(ci).\tau(1,j)=\frac{g}{b}\binom{b}{j}\quad\text{and}\quad\tau(i,1)=\frac{g}{c}\binom{c}{i}.

If ii=1, the tuple ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} is given by a single entry 11 at one of the cc vertices. The moduli space Mst​(ℙ1,ℙ2)M^{\rm st}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2}) is non-empty only if ℙ2\mathbb{P}_{2} consists only of entries 00 or 11, in which case it reduces to a point. We thus have c​(bj)c\binom{b}{j} choices for such a dimension vector contributing to the sum defining χ(1,j)​(1)\chi_{(1,j)}(1), and thus

χ(1,j)​(1)=gb​c​c​(bj)=gb​(bj),\chi_{(1,j)}(1)=\frac{g}{bc}c\binom{b}{j}=\frac{g}{b}\binom{b}{j},

confirming C5. Again, C6 follows by duality. ∎

The following proposition proves C7 and C8.

Proposition 3.6.

We have

τ⁡(i,i)=g(b−1)​(c−1)​i+g​((b−1)​(c−1)​i+gi)=∑ℓ=0∞gℓ+1​(i−1ℓ)​(i⁡(b​c−b−c)+g−1ℓ).\tau(i,i)=\frac{g}{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}{i}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}\frac{g}{\ell+1}\binom{i-1}{\ell}\binom{i(bc-b-c)+g-1}{\ell}.

We consider the central slope i=ji=j. We repeat the methods of [23, Section 11]. First we find χ(1,1)​(k)=0\chi_{(1,1)}(k)=0 for all k≥2k\geq 2, and χ(1,1)​(1)=b​c\chi_{(1,1)}(1)=bc. The defining functional equation for S(1,1)​(t)S_{(1,1)}(t) thus simplifies to

S(1,1)​(t)=(1−t​S(1,1)​(t)(b​c−b2−c2)/g)−g.S_{(1,1)}(t)=(1-tS_{(1,1)}(t)^{(bc-b^{2}-c^{2})/g})^{-g}.

Specializing [21, Theorem 1.4] to q=1q=1, we find the following: If a formal series F⁡(t)∈ℚ​⟦t⟧F(t)\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket t\rrbracket with constant term one is determined by

then it is given by

F⁡(t)=∑i≥0n(m−1)​i−n​(m​i+n−1i)​ti.F(t)=\sum_{i\geq 0}\frac{n}{(m-1)i-n}\binom{mi+n-1}{i}t^{i}.

τ⁡(i,i)=g(b​c−b−c)​i+g​((b−1)​(c−1)​i+g−1i)=g(b−1)​(c−1)​i+g​((b−1)​(c−1)​i+gi),\tau(i,i)=\frac{g}{(bc-b-c)i+g}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i+g-1}{i}=\frac{g}{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}\binom{(b-1)(c-1)i+g}{i},

confirming C7 [7, Conjecture 7]. As already noted there, C8 follows. ∎

Now we return to the general case. We first analyze the dependence of χ(d,e)​(k)\chi_{(d,e)}(k) on bb and cc.

Proposition 3.7.

There exists a polynomial P(d,e),k​(b,c)P_{(d,e),k}(b,c) of degree at most k​d−1kd-1 in bb and k​e−1ke-1 in cc such that

χ(d,e)​(k)=b​c​P(d,e),k​(b,c).\chi_{(d,e)}(k)=bcP_{(d,e),k}(b,c).

The quiver K⁡(b,c)K(b,c) has a natural Sb×ScS_{b}\times S_{c}-symmetry, which implies that the moduli space Mst​(ℙ1,ℙ2)M^{\rm st}(\mathbb{P}_{1},\mathbb{P}_{2}) only depends on the entries of ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1}, ℙ2\mathbb{P}_{2}, but not on their respective ordering. χ(d,e)​(k)=∑λ1⊢k​dλ2⊢k​eχ⁡(Mst​(λ1,λ2))​zλ1​zλ2​(bℓ⁡(λ1))​(cℓ⁡(λ2)).\chi_{(d,e)}(k)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\lambda_{1}\vdash kd}\\ {\lambda_{2}\vdash ke}\end{subarray}}\chi(M^{\rm st}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}))z_{\lambda_{1}}z_{\lambda_{2}}\binom{b}{\ell(\lambda_{1})}\binom{c}{\ell(\lambda_{2})}.

Namely, the possible ordered partitions ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{1} of k​dkd arise by choosing an unordered partition λ1\lambda_{1} of k​dkd, a derangement of λ1\lambda_{1}, and a choice of ℓ⁡(λ1)\ell(\lambda_{1}) among the bb vertices in K⁡(b,c)K(b,c) (and similarly for ℙ2\mathbb{P}_{2}). Since χ⁡(Mst​(λ1,λ2))\chi(M^{\rm st}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2})) is independent of bb and cc, we see that χ(d,e)​(k)\chi_{(d,e)}(k) behaves polynomially in bb and cc. This polynomial admits a factor b​cbc since ℓ⁡(λ1),ℓ⁡(λ2)≥1\ell(\lambda_{1}),\ell(\lambda_{2})\geq 1 for all partitions. The degree is at most k​dkd in bb and at most k​eke in cc. We can thus write

χ(d,e)​(k)=b​c​P(d,e),k​(b,c)\chi_{(d,e)}(k)=bcP_{(d,e),k}(b,c)

for some polynomial P(d,e),k​(b,c)P_{(d,e),k}(b,c) of degree at most k​d−1kd-1 in bb and k​e−1ke-1 in cc. ∎

Now we use techniques of [22, Section 4]. Essentially using [22, Lemma 4.3], we can prove: if a formal series F⁡(t)∈ℚ​⟦t⟧F(t)\in\mathbb{Q}\llbracket t\rrbracket with constant term one is determined by

F⁡(t)=∏k≥1(1−(t​F​(t))k)−ak,F(t)=\prod_{k\geq 1}(1-(tF(t))^{k})^{-a_{k}},

then, for all k∈ℚk\in\mathbb{Q}, we have

where the sum ranges over all l∗l_{*} such that ∑jj​lj=gcd⁡(i,j)\sum_{j}jl_{j}=\gcd(i,j). From direct inspection of this expression, we obtain C1:

Proposition 3.8 ([7, Conjecture 1]).

For i,j>0i,j>0, the coefficient τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) is a polynomial in b,cb,c, and gg.

4. Tight gradings

Tight gradings were introduced in [4] to give a combinatorial interpretation of the wall-function coefficients in generalized cluster scattering diagrams. In this section, we recall the definition of tight gradings and establish some of their structural properties.

4.1. Maximal Dyck paths

Fix d1,d2∈ℤ≥0d_{1},d_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. Consider a rectangle with vertices (0,0)(0,0), (0,d2)(0,d_{2}), (d1,0)(d_{1},0), and (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) with a main diagonal from (0,0)(0,0) to (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}).

We first require various notions of paths.

Definition 4.1.

Let d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} be nonnegative integers.

  • •

    A NE path is a lattice path in (ℤ×ℝ)∪(ℝ×ℤ)⊂ℝ2(\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{R})\cup(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z})\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} starting at (0,0)(0,0) and ending at (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}), proceeding by only unit north and east steps.

  • •

    A Dyck path is a NE path that never passes strictly above the main diagonal from (0,0)(0,0) to (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}).

  • •

    The maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) is the Dyck path proceeding from (0,0)(0,0) to (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) that is closest to the main diagonal.

Given a subset CC of steps (also known as edges) in a NE path 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we denote the set of east (resp. north) steps by C𝐄C_{\mathbf{E}} (resp. C𝐍C_{\mathbf{N}}) and the total number of steps by |C||C|. For edges e1∈𝒫𝐄e_{1}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} and e2∈𝒫𝐍e_{2}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}, let e1​e2→\overrightarrow{e_{1}e_{2}} denote the subpath proceeding east from the left endpoint of e1e_{1} to the top endpoint of e2e_{2}, continuing cyclically around 𝒫\mathcal{P} if e1e_{1} is east of e2e_{2}.

The Dyck paths from (0,0)(0,0) to (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) form a partially ordered set by comparing the heights at all vertices. The maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) is the maximal element under this partial order. We label the horizontal edges in 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) from left to right by u1,u2,…,ud1u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{d_{1}} and the vertical edges from bottom to top by v1,v2,…,vd2v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{d_{2}}.

Definition 4.2.

We define the function π:𝒫(d1,d2)→[0,d1+d2)\pi:\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})\to[0,d_{1}+d_{2}) by π⁡(e)≔d2​x−d1​y\rd(e)\coloneqq d_{2}x-d_{1}y for each edge ee, where (x,y)(x,y) is the location of the south or west vertex of ee.

When d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} are coprime, the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) corresponds to the lower Christoffel word of slope d2/d1d_{2}/d_{1}; see [3, Sec. 1.2] for further details. The following properties follow from this identification.

Remark 4.3.

The quantity π⁡(e)\rd(e) is the relative distance of the left (resp. bottom) vertex to the main diagonal among all vertices of 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}). In particular, we have π⁡(e)=π⁡(e′)\rd(e)=\rd(e^{\prime}) if their distances to the diagonal are equal, and we have π⁡(e)=0\rd(e)=0 if the corresponding vertex is on the main diagonal. Moreover, as in [3, Lemma 1.3], if d1d_{1} and d2d_{2} are coprime, then π⁡(e)\rd(e) is distinct for all edges of 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}).

More specifically, for each edge α\alpha of the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}), with lattice point (x,y)(x,y) as its western or southern vertex, the value π⁡(α)/d1=d2​x−d1​yd1=d2d1​x−y≥0\pi(\alpha)/d_{1}=\frac{d_{2}x-d_{1}y}{d_{1}}=\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}x-y\geq 0 since (x,y)(x,y) lies on or below the line of slope d2d1\frac{d_{2}}{d_{1}}. The fractional value is the exact distance to the diagonal. If we label the edges of 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) in order from (0,0)(0,0) to (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}) as α0,α1,α2,…,αd1+d2−1\alpha_{0},\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\dots,\alpha_{d_{1}+d_{2}-1}, this allows us to interpret π⁡(αk)\pi(\alpha_{k}) as the modular residue of k⋅d2mod(d1+d2)k\cdot d_{2}\mod(d_{1}+d_{2}).

Example 4.4.

Consider the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(5,3)\mathcal{P}(5,3) that goes through the sequence of lattice points (0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(4,1),(4,2),(5,2),(5,3)(0,0),(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(3,1),(4,1),(4,2),(5,2),(5,3) using the edges given by u1,u2,v1,u3,u4,v2,u5,v3u_{1},u_{2},v_{1},u_{3},u_{4},v_{2},u_{5},v_{3}. Then we get all distinct integer values in [0,d1+d2)[0,d_{1}+d_{2}), for d1=5d_{1}=5, d2=3d_{2}=3, as expected:

π⁡(α0)=π⁡(u1)=3⋅0−5⋅0=0\pi(\alpha_{0})=\pi(u_{1})=3\cdot 0-5\cdot 0=0       π⁡(α4)=π⁡(u4)=3⋅3−5⋅1=4\pi(\alpha_{4})=\pi(u_{4})=3\cdot 3-5\cdot 1=4

π⁡(α1)=π⁡(u2)=3⋅1−5⋅0=3\pi(\alpha_{1})=\pi(u_{2})=3\cdot 1-5\cdot 0=3       π⁡(α5)=π⁡(v2)=3⋅4−5⋅1=7\pi(\alpha_{5})=\pi(v_{2})=3\cdot 4-5\cdot 1=7

π⁡(α2)=π⁡(v1)=3⋅2−5⋅0=6\pi(\alpha_{2})=\pi(v_{1})=3\cdot 2-5\cdot 0=6       π⁡(α6)=π⁡(u5)=3⋅4−5⋅2=2\pi(\alpha_{6})=\pi(u_{5})=3\cdot 4-5\cdot 2=2

π⁡(α3)=π⁡(u3)=3⋅2−5⋅1=1\pi(\alpha_{3})=\pi(u_{3})=3\cdot 2-5\cdot 1=1       π⁡(α7)=π⁡(v3)=3⋅5−5⋅2=5\pi(\alpha_{7})=\pi(v_{3})=3\cdot 5-5\cdot 2=5

4.2. Definition of tight gradings

Motivated by Lee–Schiffler [18], Lee, Li, and Zelevinsky [17] introduced combinatorial objects called compatible pairs to construct the greedy basis for rank-22 cluster algebras, consisting of indecomposable positive elements including the cluster monomials. Rupel [24, 25] extended this construction to the setting of generalized rank-22 cluster algebras by defining compatible gradings.

A function from the set of edges on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) to ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} is called a grading. Given a grading ω:𝒫⁡(d1,d2)→ℤ≥0\omega:\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2})\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and a set of edges C⊂𝒫⁡(d1,d2)C\subset\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}), we set ω⁡(C)≔∑e∈Cω⁡(e)\omega(C)\coloneqq\sum_{e\in C}\omega(e).

Definition 4.5.

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be an NE path. A grading ω:𝒫→ℤ≥0\omega:\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} is called compatible if for every pair of u∈𝒫𝐄u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} and v∈𝒫𝐍v\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}} with ω⁡(u)​ω​(v)>0\omega(u)\omega(v)>0, there exists an edge ee along the subpath u​v→\overrightarrow{uv} so that at least one of the following holds:

(4.6) e∈𝒫𝐍∖{v}and|u​e→𝐍|=ω⁡(u​e→𝐄);\displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}\setminus\{v\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{E}}\right);
e∈𝒫𝐄∖{u}and|e​v→𝐄|=ω⁡(e​v→𝐍).\displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}\setminus\{u\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{E}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{N}}\right).

We denote the set of compatible gradings on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with ω⁡(𝒫𝐍)=p\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})=p, ω⁡(𝒫𝐄)=q\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})=q, by CG⁡(d1,d2,p,q)\CG(d_{1},d_{2},p,q). In the compatible pairs setting of [17], ω\omega takes at most one distinct nonzero value cc on the horizontal edges and at most one distinct nonzero value bb on the vertical edges. This is the setting relevant for the cluster algebra 𝒜⁡(b,c)\mathcal{A}(b,c) and the cluster scattering diagram 𝔇(b,c)\mathfrak{D}_{(b,c)}. Thus we define CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) to be the subset of gradings ω\omega in CG⁡(d1,d2,b​i,c​j)\CG(d_{1},d_{2},bi,cj) such that ω\omega is either bb (resp. cc) or 00 on each edge of 𝒫𝐍\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}} (resp. 𝒫𝐄\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}).

In their study of compatible pairs, Lee, Li, and Zelevinsky [17] introduced the notion of the “shadow” of a set of horizontal (or vertical) edges, which Rupel [25] extended to the setting of gradings.

Definition 4.7.

Fix an NE path 𝒫\mathcal{P} and a grading ω:𝒫→ℤ≥0\omega\colon\mathcal{P}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. For each edge ee in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, we define its shadow, denoted by sh⁡(e)\sh(e) or sh⁡(e,ω)\sh(e;\omega), as follows.

  • •

    If ee is horizontal, then its shadow is e​v→𝐍\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{N}}, where v∈𝒫𝐍v\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}} is chosen such that |e​v→𝐍|=ω⁡(e​v→𝐄)|\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega(\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{E}}) and e​v→\overrightarrow{ev} has minimal length under this condition. If no such vv exists, let sh⁡(e)=𝒫𝐍\sh(e)=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}.

  • •

    If ee is vertical, then its shadow is u​e→𝐄\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{E}}, where u∈𝒫𝐄u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} is chosen such that |u​e→𝐄|=ω⁡(u​e→𝐍)|\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{E}}|=\omega(\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{N}}) and u​e→\overrightarrow{ue} has minimal length under this condition. If no such uu exists, let sh⁡(e)=𝒫𝐄\sh(e)=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}.

For C⊂𝒫C\subset\mathcal{P}, let the shadow of CC be sh⁡(C)=⋃e∈Csh⁡(e)\sh(C)=\bigcup_{e\in C}\sh(e).

Let S𝐄=S𝐄​(ω)S_{\mathbf{E}}=S_{\mathbf{E}}(\omega) denote the set of horizontal edges u∈𝒫𝐄u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} such that ω⁡(u)>0\omega(u)>0. Similarly, we define S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} to be the set of vertical edges with nonzero value in the grading.

Definition 4.8 (tight grading).

A compatible grading ω\omega in CG⁡(d1,d2,p,q)\CG(d_{1},d_{2},p,q) is called tight if

  • •

    S𝐄⊆sh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) or S𝐍⊆sh⁡(S𝐄)S_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}) and

  • •

    p​d2−q​d1=ϵ​gcd⁡(p,q)pd_{2}-qd_{1}=\epsilon\gcd(p,q) for ϵ=1\epsilon=1 or −1-1.

Remark 4.9.

The two bulleted conditions in Definition 4.8 each have two possibilities, but the choice of one determines the other. In particular, given a tight grading, we have S𝐄⊆sh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) if and only if ϵ=1\epsilon=1, and otherwise we have S𝐍⊆sh⁡(S𝐄)S_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}) when ϵ=−1\epsilon=-1 (see, for example, [5, Lemma 5.23]).

We now explain how tight gradings are related to wall-functions. Returning to the scattering diagram 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}) at the beginning of Section 2 where

Pi=1+∑k≥1pi,k​xik∈𝕜⁡⟦xi⟧.P_{i}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{i,k}x_{i}^{k}\in\Bbbk\llbracket x_{i}\rrbracket.

A main result of [5] is the following integrality and positivity statement for 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}): any wall-function coefficient behaves as a polynomial in {pi,k∣i∈{1,2},k≥1}\{p_{i,k}\mid i\in\{1,2\},k\geq 1\} with nonnegative integer coefficients given by counts of tight gradings.

Theorem 4.10 ([5, Theorem 5.17 and (5.35)]).
  1. (1)

    There are nonnegative integers λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) for pairs of partitions (𝐏1,𝐏2)(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) such that for any positive integers dd and ee with gcd⁡(d,e)=1\gcd(d,e)=1, the wall-function on ℝ≤0​(d,e)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e) is given by

    𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)=1+∑k≥1∑𝐏1⊢k​d∑𝐏2⊢k​eλ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)​∏i∈𝐏1p1,i​∏j∈𝐏2p2,j⋅x1k​d​x2k​e.\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash kd}\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash ke}\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\prod_{i\in\mathbf{P}_{1}}p_{1,i}\prod_{j\in\mathbf{P}_{2}}p_{2,j}\cdot x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}.
  2. (2)

    For partitions 𝐏1⊢p\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash p and 𝐏2⊢q\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash q, the number λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) counts tight gradings ω\omega on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with p​d2−q​d1=±gcd⁡(p,q)pd_{2}-qd_{1}=\pm\gcd(p,q), d1≥pd_{1}\geq p, d2≥qd_{2}\geq q such that

    𝐏1=(ω⁡(v)∣v∈S𝐍​(ω))and𝐏2=(ω⁡(u)∣u∈S𝐄​(ω)),\mathbf{P}_{1}=(\omega(v)\mid v\in S_{\mathbf{N}}(\omega))\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{P}_{2}=(\omega(u)\mid u\in S_{\mathbf{E}}(\omega)),

    independent of the choice of (d1,d2)(d_{1},d_{2}). Here, we reorder the non-zero elements of the tuples (ω⁡(v)∣v∈S𝐍​(ω))(\omega(v)\mid v\in S_{\mathbf{N}}(\omega)) and (ω⁡(u)∣u∈S𝐄​(ω))(\omega(u)\mid u\in S_{\mathbf{E}}(\omega)) in weakly decreasing order so that they are integer partitions.

Remark 4.11.

In the cluster setting, Theorem 4.10 states that

τb,c​(i,j)=|{ω∈CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)∣ω​ is a tight grading}|,\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\left|\left\{\omega\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j)\mid\omega\text{ is a tight grading}\right\}\right|\,,

whenever d1≥b​id_{1}\geq bi, d2≥c​jd_{2}\geq cj, and |b​i​d2−c​j​d1|=gcd⁡(b​i,c​j)|bid_{2}-cjd_{1}|=\gcd(bi,cj).

4.3. Structure of Tight Gradings

We now prove several structural results about tight gradings, which are needed for the later combinatorial constructions.

We begin by establishing that tight gradings have only one “component”, in the sense that the horizontal and vertical shadows have no gaps.

Lemma 4.12.

Let ω\omega be a tight grading on 𝒫=𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with ω⁡(𝒫𝐍)=p\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})=p and ω⁡(𝒫𝐄)=q\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})=q. Then there exists a unique umax∈𝒫𝐄u_{\max}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} and vmax∈𝒫𝐍v_{\max}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}} such that

  • •

    umax​vmax→=sh⁡(S𝐄)∪sh⁡(S𝐍)∪{vmax}\overrightarrow{u_{\max}v_{\max}}=\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}})\cup\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}})\cup\{v_{\max}\} if p​d2−q​d1>0pd_{2}-qd_{1}>0, or

  • •

    umax​vmax→={umax}∪sh⁡(S𝐄)∪sh⁡(S𝐍)\overrightarrow{u_{\max}v_{\max}}=\{u_{\max}\}\cup\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}})\cup\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) if p​d2−q​d1<0pd_{2}-qd_{1}<0.

Proof.

Let γ≔gcd⁡(p,q)=|p​d2−q​d1|\gamma\coloneqq\gcd(p,q)=|pd_{2}-qd_{1}|. Without loss of generality, assume p​d2−q​d1<0pd_{2}-qd_{1}<0. The case where p​d2−q​d1>0pd_{2}-qd_{1}>0 is analogous as we can swap the roles of horizontal and vertical edges. Pick u(i)∈S𝐄u^{(i)}\in S_{\mathbf{E}} for i=1,2,…,ℓi=1,2,\dots,\ell such that sh⁡(S𝐄)\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}) is the disjoint union of the shadows sh⁡(u(i))\sh(u^{(i)}). Note that this is possible since edge shadows are either nested or disjoint. For each ii, let v(i)v^{(i)} be the unique vertical edge such that u(i)​v(i)→𝐍=sh⁡(u(i))\displaystyle\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}}_{\mathbf{N}}=\sh(u^{(i)}). Let πi≔π⁡(u(i))\pi_{i}\coloneqq\pi\left(u^{(i)}\right), qi≔|u(i)​v(i)→𝐍|q_{i}\coloneqq\left|\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}}_{\mathbf{N}}\right|, and pi≔|u(i)​v(i)→𝐄|−1p_{i}\coloneqq\left|\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}}_{\mathbf{E}}\right|-1.

By the definition of compatibility for the grading ω\omega, we have qi​d1>pi​d2+πi≥pi​d2q_{i}d_{1}>p_{i}d_{2}+\pi_{i}\geq p_{i}d_{2}. Moreover, since ∑i=1ℓqi=q\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}q_{i}=q and q​d1−p​d2=gcd⁡(p,q)qd_{1}-pd_{2}=\gcd(p,q), we can choose a partition (η1,…,ηℓ)⊢γ(\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{\ell})\vdash\gamma such that pi=ηiγ​pp_{i}=\frac{\eta_{i}}{\gamma}p and qi=ηiγ​qq_{i}=\frac{\eta_{i}}{\gamma}q. In particular, this implies πi<qi​d1−pi​d2=ηi\pi_{i}<q_{i}d_{1}-p_{i}d_{2}=\eta_{i}.

We now aim to show that u1∈u(i)​v(i)→u_{1}\in\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}} for all ii. Consider the horizontal edge ee that is πi​pγ\pi_{i}\frac{p}{\gamma} steps to the right of u(i)u^{(i)} (continuing cyclically around 𝒫\mathcal{P} if necessary). We then have

π⁡(e)=πi+πi​pγ​d2−πi​qγ​d1=πi+πi⋅p​d2−q​d1γ=πi−πi=0.\pi(e)=\pi_{i}+\frac{\pi_{i}p}{\gamma}d_{2}-\frac{\pi_{i}q}{\gamma}d_{1}=\pi_{i}+\pi_{i}\cdot\frac{pd_{2}-qd_{1}}{\gamma}=\pi_{i}-\pi_{i}=0\,.

So indeed, since πi​pγ<pi\pi_{i}\frac{p}{\gamma}<p_{i} and u1u_{1} is the unique edge with π⁡(e)=0\pi(e)=0, the edge u1u_{1} is included in the path u(i)​v(i)→\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}}.

As we assumed the paths u(i)​v(i)→\overrightarrow{u^{(i)}v^{(i)}} were disjoint, there can be only one such path, so ℓ=1\ell=1. We can then let umax=u(1)u_{\max}=u^{(1)}. We can also see that |sh⁡(umax)|=p+1|\sh(u_{\max})|=p+1, so we can let vmax=v(1)v_{\max}=v^{(1)}. ∎

Next, we show that the tight gradings can only be located at certain positions along the Dyck path; this result is developed pictorially in Section 5.

Lemma 4.13.

Let ω\omega be a tight grading on 𝒫=𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with ω⁡(𝒫𝐍)=p\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}})=p and ω⁡(𝒫𝐄)=q\omega(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}})=q, and set γ=gcd⁡(p,q)\gamma=\gcd(p,q). Let umaxu_{\max} and vmaxv_{\max} be as in Lemma 4.12. Let vminv_{\min} be the first vertical edge to the right of umaxu_{\max}, and let uminu_{\min} be the first horizontal edge below vmaxv_{\max}.

  • •

    If p​d2−q​d1>0pd_{2}-qd_{1}>0, we have d1≤π⁡(vmax)<d1+γd_{1}\leq\rd(v_{\max})<d_{1}+\gamma, π⁡(umax)=π⁡(vmax)−γ\rd(u_{\max})=\rd(v_{\max})-\gamma, and ω⁡(vmin)=0\omega(v_{\min})=0.

  • •

    If p​d2−q​d1<0pd_{2}-qd_{1}<0, we have 0≤π⁡(umax)<γ0\leq\rd(u_{\max})<\gamma, π⁡(vmax)=π⁡(umax)+d1+d2−γ\rd(v_{\max})=\rd(u_{\max})+d_{1}+d_{2}-\gamma, and ω⁡(umin)=0\omega(u_{\min})=0.

Proof.

By definition, since ω\omega is a tight grading, either S𝐄⊂sh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subset\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) or S𝐍⊂sh⁡(S𝐄)S_{\mathbf{N}}\subset\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}) holds. Assume S𝐄⊂sh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subset\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}), so by Remark 4.9, we are in the case where p​d2−q​d1>0pd_{2}-qd_{1}>0.

The subpath 𝔰=umax​vmax→\mathfrak{s}=\overrightarrow{u_{\max}v_{\max}} contains all edges in sh⁡(umax)\sh(u_{\max}), and its set of horizontal edges is precisely sh⁡(vmax)\sh(v_{\max}). Moreover, note that vmax∉sh⁡(S𝐄)v_{\max}\notin\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}). Therefore 𝔰\mathfrak{s} contains exactly pp horizontal edges and contains at least q+1q+1 vertical edges. Hence we have

(4.14) π⁡(vmax)−π⁡(umax)=|𝔰𝐄|​d2−(|𝔰𝐍|−1)​d1=p​d2−(|𝔰𝐍|−1)​d1≤p​d2−q​d1=γ.\pi(v_{\max})-\pi(u_{\max})=|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{E}}|d_{2}-(|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{N}}|-1)d_{1}=pd_{2}-(|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{N}}|-1)d_{1}\leq pd_{2}-qd_{1}=\gamma\,.

As the edge vmaxv_{\max} is vertical, we have π⁡(vmax)≥d1\pi(v_{\max})\geq d_{1}. So π⁡(umax)≥d1−γ\pi(u_{\max})\geq d_{1}-\gamma. Moreover, since π⁡(vmax)>π⁡(umax)\pi(v_{\max})>\pi(u_{\max}), we have

p​d2−(|𝔰𝐍|−1)​d1=γ−(|𝔰𝐍|−(q+1))​d1>0.pd_{2}-(|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{N}}|-1)d_{1}=\gamma-(|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{N}}|-(q+1))d_{1}>0\,.

Then γ≤d1\gamma\leq d_{1} implies that |𝔰𝐍|=q+1|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{N}}|=q+1. So the inequality in Equation 4.14 is actually an equality, hence π⁡(umax)=π⁡(vmax)−γ\pi(u_{\max})=\pi(v_{\max})-\gamma.

Since π⁡(umax)≥d1−γ≥d1−d2\pi(u_{\max})\geq d_{1}-\gamma\geq d_{1}-d_{2}, the edge ee immediately to the right of umaxu_{\max} must be vertical, as π⁡(e)≥d1\pi(e)\geq d_{1}. Hence vminv_{\min} is immediately to the right of umaxu_{\max}. In order for ω\omega to be compatible, we must have ω⁡(vmin)=0\omega(v_{\min})=0 since ω⁡(umax)>0\omega(u_{\max})>0.

The case p​d2−q​d1<0pd_{2}-qd_{1}<0 proceeds similarly, where we still consider the subpath 𝔰=umax​vmax→\mathfrak{s}=\overrightarrow{u_{\max}v_{\max}}. Now 𝔰\mathfrak{s} contains exactly qq vertical edges and at least p+1p+1 horizontal edges, so we have

(4.15) π⁡(vmax)−π⁡(umax)=|𝔰𝐄|​d2−(q−1)​d1≥(p+1)​d2−(q−1)​d1=d1+d2−γ.\pi(v_{\max})-\pi(u_{\max})=|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{E}}|d_{2}-(q-1)d_{1}\geq(p+1)d_{2}-(q-1)d_{1}=d_{1}+d_{2}-\gamma\,.

Since π⁡(vmax)<d1+d2\pi(v_{\max})<d_{1}+d_{2}, we have π⁡(umax)<γ\pi(u_{\max})<\gamma. As before, Equation 4.15 also implies that |𝔰𝐄|=p+1|\mathfrak{s}_{\mathbf{E}}|=p+1, so π⁡(vmax)=π⁡(umax)+d1+d2−γ\pi(v_{\max})=\pi(u_{\max})+d_{1}+d_{2}-\gamma. The edge ee immediately preceding vmaxv_{\max} has π⁡(e)=d1−γ<d1\pi(e)=d_{1}-\gamma<d_{1}, so e=umine=u_{\min}. We then have ω⁡(umin)=0\omega(u_{\min})=0 since ω⁡(vmax)>0\omega(v_{\max})>0. ∎

The fact that certain edges must have value 00 in the tight grading is needed later to demonstrate the Weyl symmetry in terms of tight gradings (see Section 7).

Corollary 4.16.

If 𝐏1=(p)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(p) and 𝐏2=(q)\mathbf{P}_{2}=(q), then λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)=gcd⁡(p,q)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})=\gcd(p,q). The corresponding tight gradings are such that the unique edges u∈S𝐄u\in S_{\mathbf{E}} and v∈S𝐍v\in S_{\mathbf{N}} satisfy π⁡(u)=ℓ\pi(u)=\ell and π⁡(v)=d1+d2−gcd⁡(p,q)+π⁡(u)\pi(v)=d_{1}+d_{2}-\gcd(p,q)+\pi(u) for any 0≤ℓ<gcd⁡(p,q)0\leq\ell<\gcd(p,q).

Proof.

This follows directly from Lemma 4.13 by noting that umaxu_{\max} and vmaxv_{\max} are the only edges with nonzero value in any such tight grading. ∎

In the next section, we describe a way to visualize tight gradings that captures these structural results.

5. A pictorial description of tight gradings via tiling

In this section, we give a pictorial description of tight gradings as partial tilings bounded by the underlying Dyck path and a rectangular frame. This serves not only as a helpful tool in constructing tight gradings, but also allows for comparisons of the relative “tightness” of gradings.

Throughout this section, we fix (d1,d2,p,q)(d_{1},d_{2},p,q) such that γ=|p​d2−q​d1|=gcd⁡(p,q)\gamma=|pd_{2}-qd_{1}|=\gcd(p,q).

5.1. Frames

First we consider the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}). By considering the doubled Dyck path, we eliminate the need to consider the cyclic nature of the compatibility conditions when constructing tight gradings. Thus we consider 𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}) as an “unwrapping” of 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}).

Example 5.1.

As a running example, let (d1,d2,p,q)=(14,9,12,8)(d_{1},d_{2},p,q)=(14,9,12,8). The maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)=𝒫⁡(28,18)\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2})=\mathcal{P}(28,18) is given in Figure 1, along with the four points in PP. Note that this is two copies of the Dyck path 𝒫⁡(14,9)\mathcal{P}(14,9) glued end-to-end.

Let P={p0,p1,…,pγ−1}P=\{p_{0},p_{1},...,p_{\gamma-1}\} be the set of the γ\gamma points on the first half of 𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}) that are closest to the main diagonal. We label these such that π⁡(em)=m<γ\pi(e_{m})=m<\gamma where eme_{m} is the horizontal edge immediately to the right of pmp_{m}. Note that p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0) lies on the main diagonal, but none of the other (γ−1)(\gamma-1) points in PP lie on the main diagonal. In fact, the modular description of the Dyck path allows us to explicitly calculate the positions of the vertices pmp_{m}. For 1≤m<γ1\leq m<\gamma, we have

pm=(d1−m⋅pγ,d2−m⋅qγ).p_{m}=\left(d_{1}-m\cdot\frac{p}{\gamma},d_{2}-m\cdot\frac{q}{\gamma}\right)\,.
Remark 5.2.

By Lemma 4.12 and Lemma 4.13, any tight grading on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) is such that the left vertex of umaxu_{\max} (when q​d1>p​d2qd_{1}>pd_{2}) or the top vertex of vmaxv_{\max} (when p​d2>q​d1pd_{2}>qd_{1}) is among the vertices in PP.

Fix some 𝔭∈P\mathfrak{p}\in P. When q​d1>p​d2qd_{1}>pd_{2}, let L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} be the (p+1)×q(p+1)\times q rectangular frame whose southwestern vertex is at 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. When p​d2>q​d1pd_{2}>qd_{1}, let L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} be the p×(q+1)p\times(q+1) rectangular frame whose northeastern vertex is at 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. Let 𝒟𝔭\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{p}} be the portion of the path 𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}) contained in L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}}.

Example 5.3.

When 𝔭=p2=(8,5)∈P\mathfrak{p}=p_{2}=(8,5)\in P, the frame L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} is given in Figure 2.

5.2. Construction of footprints associated to ur(s)u_{r}^{(s)}

Let ω\omega be a grading on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with ω⁡(S𝐍)=p\omega(S_{\mathbf{N}})=p and ω⁡(S𝐄)=q\omega(S_{\mathbf{E}})=q. Let ω𝔭\omega_{\mathfrak{p}} be the grading on 𝒟𝔭\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{p}} obtained by assigning an edge e∈𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)e\in\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}) the value of ω\omega on the unique edge e′e^{\prime} of 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with π⁡(e′)=π⁡(e)\pi(e^{\prime})=\pi(e), then restricting to 𝒟𝔭⊂𝒫⁡(2​d1,2​d2)\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{p}}\subset\mathcal{P}(2d_{1},2d_{2}).

Let u1(1),u1(2),…,u1(σ)u_{1}^{(1)},u_{1}^{(2)},\dots,u_{1}^{(\sigma)} be the set of horizontal edges uu in 𝒟𝔭\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{p}} such that ω𝔭​(u)>0\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(u)>0, ordered from left-to-right. For s∈{1,2,…,σ}s\in\{1,2,\dots,\sigma\}, let ρs\rho_{s} denote the number of horizontal edges strictly to the left of u1(s)u_{1}^{(s)} in 𝒟𝔭\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{p}}. We define ℱ𝐄​(L𝔭,ω)\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{E}}(L_{\mathfrak{p}},\omega), which is a set of unit horizontal edges inside L𝔭∩(ℝ×ℤ)L_{\mathfrak{p}}\cap(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{Z}) given by

ℱ𝐄​(L𝔭,ω)={ur(s):s∈{1,2,…,σ}​ and ​r∈{1,2,…,ρs+1}}.\mathcal{F}_{\mathbf{E}}(L_{\mathfrak{p}},\omega)=\{u_{r}^{(s)}\,:\,s\in\{1,2,...,\sigma\}\text{ and }r\in\{1,2,...,\rho_{s}+1\}\}\,.

The footprint (or tile) of each ur(s)u_{r}^{(s)} is defined to be the 1×ω⁡(u1(s))1\times\omega(u_{1}^{(s)}) rectangle whose south edge is ur(s)u_{r}^{(s)}. For r>1r>1, the edge ur(s)u_{r}^{(s)} is defined via the following double inductive process:

∙\bullet The base case: By Lemma 4.13, we have ρ1=0\rho_{1}=0. Thus, the base case of r=1r=1 consists of the construction of u1(1)u_{1}^{(1)} as above.

∙\bullet The outer inductive hypothesis: suppose that u1(s),u2(s),…,uρs+1(s)u_{1}^{(s)},u_{2}^{(s)},\dots,u_{\rho_{s}+1}^{(s)} are constructed for some s∈{1,2,…,σ}s\in\{1,2,\dots,\sigma\}.

∙\bullet The inner inductive hypothesis: Suppose that u1(s+1),u2(s+1),…,uℓ(s+1)u_{1}^{(s+1)},u_{2}^{(s+1)},\dots,u_{\ell}^{(s+1)} are constructed for some ℓ∈{1,2,…,ρs+1+1}\ell\in\{1,2,\dots,\rho_{s+1}+1\}.

∙\bullet The base step of the inner induction : construct u1(s+1)u_{1}^{(s+1)}, as described above.

∙\bullet The inductive step of the inner induction : ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} is uniquely determined by the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} in the column directly to the left of ur(s+1)u_{r}^{(s+1)};

  2. (2)

    Either

    1. (a)

      ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} is Northwest of ur(s+1)u_{r}^{(s+1)}, in which case its footprint is colored cyan; or

    2. (b)

      ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} is directly to the West of ur(s+1)u_{r}^{(s+1)}, in which case its footprint is colored dark blue;

    and ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} is as far South as possible, while the interior of the footprint of ur+1(s+1)u_{r+1}^{(s+1)} does not overlap with the footprint of ur′(s′)u_{r^{\prime}}^{(s^{\prime})} for r′≤rr^{\prime}\leq r or s′≤ss^{\prime}\leq s.

We define DarkBlue​(w)\text{DarkBlue}(w) as the union of the interior of dark blue tiles, and Cyan​(w)\text{Cyan}(w) as the union of the interior of cyan tiles.

5.4. Reinterpretation of tight gradings

We now describe tight gradings purely in terms of their footprints. This gives a visual tool for constructing and classifying tight gradings.

Proposition 5.8.

The grading ω\omega is tight if and only if there is some 𝔭∈P\mathfrak{p}\in P such that ω𝔭​(S𝐍)=p\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{N}})=p, ω𝔭​(S𝐄)=q\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{E}})=q, and

Red⁡(w)∩Cyan⁡(w)=Red⁡(w)∩DarkBlue⁡(w)=DarkRed⁡(w)∩Cyan⁡(w)=∅.\mathrm{Red}(w)\cap\mathrm{Cyan}(w)=\mathrm{Red}(w)\cap\mathrm{DarkBlue}(w)=\mathrm{DarkRed}(w)\cap\mathrm{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing.
Remark 5.9.

Note that dark blue and dark red footprints are allowed to intersect. We depict this intersection in purple. We combine the purple regions according to the following rule: the intersection of ur1(s1)u_{r_{1}}^{(s_{1})} and vr2(s2)v_{r_{2}}^{(s_{2})} is in the same purple component as the intersection of ur1′(s1′)u_{r_{1}^{\prime}}^{(s_{1}^{\prime})} and vr2′(s2′)v_{r_{2}^{\prime}}^{(s_{2}^{\prime})} if and only if s1=s1′s_{1}=s_{1}^{\prime} and s2=s2′s_{2}=s_{2}^{\prime}.

Before presenting the proof of Proposition 5.8, we illustrate the construction in some examples.

Example 5.10.

Continue from Examples 5.5 and 5.7. See the picture below. Since

Red⁡(w)∩Cyan⁡(w)=Red⁡(w)∩DarkBlue⁡(w)=DarkRed⁡(w)∩Cyan⁡(w)=∅,\mathrm{Red}(w)\cap\mathrm{Cyan}(w)=\mathrm{Red}(w)\cap\mathrm{DarkBlue}(w)=\mathrm{DarkRed}(w)\cap\mathrm{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing,

the grading ω\omega is tight.

Proof of Proposition 5.8.

Let ω\omega be a grading and 𝔭∈P\mathfrak{p}\in P such that ω𝔭​(S𝐍)=p\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{N}})=p and ω𝔭​(S𝐄)=q\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{E}})=q. Suppose that Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)≠∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)\neq\varnothing.

A rectangle in L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} whose vertices are lattice points and whose edges are vertical or horizontal will be called a lattice rectangle. A lattice rectangle whose southwestern corner and northeastern corner lie on the maximal Dyck path will be called a Dyck rectangle. For a Dyck rectangle RR in L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} whose northwestern vertex is at (xW,yN)(x_{W},y_{N}), let bRb_{R} be the interior of the unit square whose vertices are at (xW−1/2±1/2,yN−1/2±1/2)(x_{W}-1/2\pm 1/2,y_{N}-1/2\pm 1/2).

Let T⊆L𝔭T\subseteq L_{\mathfrak{p}} be a Dyck rectangle such that Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)∩T=bT\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)\cap T=b_{T}. Let uu be the horizontal edge whose left endpoint is at the southwestern corner of TT. Let vv be the vertical edge whose upper endpoint is at the northeastern corner of TT. Then for any edge ee along the subpath u​v→\overrightarrow{uv}, none of the following holds:

e∈𝒫𝐍∖{v}and|u​e→𝐍|=ω⁡(u​e→𝐄);\displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}}\setminus\{v\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{N}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ue}_{\mathbf{E}}\right);
e∈𝒫𝐄∖{u}and|e​v→𝐄|=ω⁡(e​v→𝐍).\displaystyle e\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}}\setminus\{u\}\quad\text{and}\quad|\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{E}}|=\omega\left(\overrightarrow{ev}_{\mathbf{N}}\right).

So ω\omega is not compatible, hence not tight.

Next suppose that Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing but Red​(w)∩DarkBlue​(w)≠∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{DarkBlue}(w)\neq\varnothing. Let T⊆L𝔭T\subseteq L_{\mathfrak{p}} be a Dyck rectangle such that Red​(w)∩DarkBlue​(w)∩T=bT\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{DarkBlue}(w)\cap T=b_{T}. Let uu be the horizontal edge whose left endpoint is at the southwestern corner of TT. Let vv be the vertical edge whose upper endpoint is at the northeastern corner of TT. For any dark blue tile, there is a cyan tile that is to the right of the dark blue tile. Hence Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)≠∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)\neq\varnothing, which is a contradiction. This means that if Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing then Red​(w)∩DarkBlue​(w)=∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{DarkBlue}(w)=\varnothing, and by symmetry, DarkRed​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=∅\text{DarkRed}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing.

Therefore, if ω\omega is tight, then Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=Red​(w)∩DarkBlue​(w)=DarkRed​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{DarkBlue}(w)=\text{DarkRed}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing.

The converse is straightforward, because if Red​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=Red​(w)∩DarkBlue​(w)=DarkRed​(w)∩Cyan​(w)=∅\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\text{Red}(w)\cap\text{DarkBlue}(w)=\text{DarkRed}(w)\cap\text{Cyan}(w)=\varnothing then for every pair of u∈𝒫𝐄u\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{E}} and v∈𝒫𝐍v\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{N}} with ω⁡(u)​ω​(v)>0\omega(u)\omega(v)>0, it is easy to find an edge ee along the subpath u​v→\overrightarrow{uv} so that at least one of (4.6) holds. The condition that there is some choice of 𝔭∈P\mathfrak{p}\in P such that ω𝔭​(S𝐍)=p\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{N}})=p and ω𝔭​(S𝐄)=q\omega_{\mathfrak{p}}(S_{\mathbf{E}})=q is necessary by Remark 5.2. ∎

Remark 5.12.

The red and cyan tiles are precisely the tiles that appear in the tiling construction described in [4] and [5]. For any horizontal edge on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}), the total height of the cyan tiles in the column above it is precisely the size of its local shadow, and analogously for the red tiles in the row containing each vertical edge. The dark red and dark blue tiles (as well as their purple intersection) did not appear in any of the previous tiling constructions.

6. Proof of Theorem 1.2

Recall the general scattering diagram 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}) at the beginning of Section 2 with

Pi=1+∑k≥1pi,k​xik∈𝕜⁡⟦xi⟧.P_{i}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{i,k}x_{i}^{k}\in\Bbbk\llbracket x_{i}\rrbracket.

By treating pi,kp_{i,k} as indeterminates, we regard 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}) as a kind of universal scattering diagram since any scattering diagram in the context of Section 2 can be specialized from 𝔇⁡(P1,P2)\mathfrak{D}(P_{1},P_{2}) by taking particular values of pi,kp_{i,k} in 𝕜\Bbbk; see [5, Section 5.6] for an algebraic formalization. Now part (1) of Theorem 1.2 readily follows from Theorem 4.10 via specialization.

Proof of Theorem 1.2(1).

The scattering diagram 𝔇(c,b)∘=𝔇⁡((1+x1)c,(1+x2)b)\mathfrak{D}^{\circ}_{(c,b)}=\mathfrak{D}((1+x_{1})^{c},(1+x_{2})^{b}) is obtained from specializing the universal scattering diagram at

p1,k=(ck)andp2,k=(bk).p_{1,k}=\binom{c}{k}\quad\text{and}\quad p_{2,k}=\binom{b}{k}.

By the formula of 𝔣ℝ≤0​(d,e)\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(d,e)} given in Theorem 4.10, we see that

ϱk=ϱ⁡(k​d,k​e)=∑𝐏1⊢k​d∑𝐏2⊢k​eλ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)​∏p∈𝐏1(cp)​∏q∈𝐏2(bq).\varrho_{k}=\varrho(kd,ke)=\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash kd}\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash ke}\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})\prod_{p\in\mathbf{P}_{1}}\binom{c}{p}\prod_{q\in\mathbf{P}_{2}}\binom{b}{q}.

Clearly ϱk\varrho_{k} is a polynomial in bb and cc, and b​cbc divides ϱk\varrho_{k}.

By Corollary 4.16, the leading term λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) for 𝐏1=(k​d)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(kd) and 𝐏2=(k​e)\mathbf{P}_{2}=(ke) equals k=gcd⁡(k​d,k​e)k=\gcd(kd,ke). ∎

Now that the polynomiality of ϱk\varrho_{k} is proven, the polynomiality of τk\tau_{k} (Theorem 1.2(2)) is obtained through the change-of-lattice transformation in Proposition 2.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.2(2).

The claimed expression of τk\tau_{k} in terms of ϱk\varrho_{k} is a direct consequence of

1+∑k≥1τk​x1k​d​x2k​e=(1+∑k≥1ϱk​x1k​d​x2k​e)g/b​c(by Proposition 2.5).1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau_{k}x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}=\left(1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\varrho_{k}x_{1}^{kd}x_{2}^{ke}\right)^{g/bc}\quad\text{(by \lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{prop: change of lattice})}.

Since every ϱk\varrho_{k} is divided by b​cbc, we have τk∈ℚ⁡[b,c,g]\tau_{k}\in\mathbb{Q}[b,c,g]. The top-degree term of τk\tau_{k} in gg is given by

(ϱ1b​c)k​gk.\left(\frac{\varrho_{1}}{bc}\right)^{k}g^{k}.

As ϱ1\varrho_{1} is always non-zero by Theorem 1.2(1), the degree of τk\tau_{k} in gg is kk. ∎

Now write τk\tau_{k} as a polynomial in gg:

τk=∑n=1kτk​(n)​gn,τk​(n)∈ℚ⁡[b,c].\tau_{k}=\sum_{n=1}^{k}\tau_{k}(n)g^{n},\quad\tau_{k}(n)\in\mathbb{Q}[b,c].

Before showing Theorem 1.2(3), we first prove Theorem 1.2(4):

τk(n)=1n!∑k1+⋯+kn=kτk1(1)⋯τkn(1).\tau_{k}(n)=\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{k_{1}+\cdots+k_{n}=k}\tau_{k_{1}}(1)\cdots\tau_{k_{n}}(1).

It is another algebraic consequence directly from the change-of-lattice transformation (Proposition 2.5).

Proof of Theorem 1.2(4).

For fixed dd and ee, define the generating function

F⁡(x)≔1+∑k≥1ϱk​xk.F(x)\coloneqq 1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\varrho_{k}x^{k}.

By Proposition 2.5, we have

1+∑k≥1τk​xk=F​(x)g/b​c=exp⁡(g​ln⁡F⁡(x)b​c).1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau_{k}x^{k}=F(x)^{g/bc}=\exp\left(g\frac{\ln F(x)}{bc}\right).

Expand both sides as series of gg:

1+∑n≥1gn​∑k≥1τk​(n)​xk=1+∑n≥1gn​1n!​(ln⁡F⁡(x)b​c)n.1+\sum_{n\geq 1}g^{n}\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau_{k}(n)x^{k}=1+\sum_{n\geq 1}g^{n}\frac{1}{n!}\left(\frac{\ln F(x)}{bc}\right)^{n}.

Comparing the gng^{n}-coefficients between both sides, we have for any n≥1n\geq 1,

∑k≥1τk​(n)​xk=1n!​(∑k≥1τk​(1)​xk)n.\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau_{k}(n)x^{k}=\frac{1}{n!}\left(\sum_{k\geq 1}\tau_{k}(1)x^{k}\right)^{n}.

Comparing the xkx^{k}-coefficients of both sides yields the desired equality. ∎

Remark 6.1.

Evaluating g=b​cg=bc recovers ϱk\varrho_{k} from τk\tau_{k} by

ϱk=∑n=1k(b​c)n​τk​(n).\varrho_{k}=\sum_{n=1}^{k}(bc)^{n}\tau_{k}(n).

In particular, in the coprime case we have ϱ⁡(d,e)=b​cg​τ​(d,e)\varrho(d,e)=\frac{bc}{g}\tau(d,e).

We proceed to prove part (3) of Theorem 1.2. Write (i,j)=(k​d,k​e)(i,j)=(kd,ke) and thus τk=τ⁡(i,j)\tau_{k}=\tau(i,j). It is clear from Theorem 1.2(2) that

(6.2) degb⁡τ⁡(i,j)≤k​e−1=j−1anddegc⁡τ⁡(i,j)≤k​d−1=i−1.\deg_{b}\tau(i,j)\leq ke-1=j-1\quad\text{and}\quad\deg_{c}\tau(i,j)\leq kd-1=i-1.

We show these degree bound are attained using a tight grading interpretation. We look at “limits” of tight gradings, in the sense that at least one of bb or cc is taken to be arbitrarily large.

Lemma 6.3.

The function τ⁡(i,j)∈ℚ⁡[b,c,g]\tau(i,j)\in\mathbb{Q}[b,c,g] has degree j−1j-1 in bb and i−1i-1 in cc. Moreover, the coefficient of g​bj−1​ci−1gb^{j-1}c^{i-1} in τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) is positive.

Proof.

Fix ii, jj, and gg. We can hold these constant by choosing a suitable sequence of pairs (b,c)(b,c) tending to infinity in both entries. We view τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j) as the number of tight gradings in CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) for an appropriate choice of d1,d2d_{1},d_{2}, following Remark 4.11. (Recall that CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) is the subset of CG⁡(d1,d2,b​i,c​j)\CG(d_{1},d_{2},bi,cj) such that ω\omega takes at most one distinct nonzero value on the horizontal edges and at most one distinct nonzero value on the vertical edges.) We then fix a frame L𝔭L_{\mathfrak{p}} in 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}), as defined in Section 5.1. There is a constant number of choices of frame, namely g⋅gcd⁡(i,j)=gcd⁡(b​i,c​j)g\cdot\gcd(i,j)=\gcd(bi,cj), according to Lemma 4.13. Moreover, Lemma 4.13 guarantees that the leftmost horizontal edge in S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} and the topmost vertical edge in S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} are fixed by the choice of frame. Since the j−1j-1 additional horizontal edges of S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} must be chosen from the remaining i​b−1ib-1 edges in the horizontal shadow, the degree in bb is at most j−1j-1. Similarly the degree in cc is at most i−1i-1.

Suppose we choose the i−1i-1 other vertical edges in S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} arbitrarily among the c2\frac{c}{2} topmost vertical edges within the rectangular support. There are (c/2i−1)\binom{c/2}{i-1} such choices. The red and dark red tiles in the second-to-topmost row have total length (i−1)​b(i-1)b and is horizontal distance at most i​b2​j±o⁡(b)\frac{ib}{2j}\pm o(b) from the topmost vertical edge. Thus, there are b−i​b2​j±o⁡(b)b-\frac{ib}{2j}\pm o(b) columns that do not have any red or dark red tiles except in the topmost row. Hence the remaining j−1j-1 edges of S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} may be picked arbitrarily among the (1−i2​j)​b\left(1-\frac{i}{2j}\right)b leftmost unchosen horizontal edges in the support. Note that there are no red or dark red tiles in these leftmost (1−i2​j)​b\left(1-\frac{i}{2j}\right)b columns except for in the topmost row, so there are no overlaps between tiles and hence no purple tiles arise. There are ((1−i2​j)​bj−1)\binom{\left(1-\frac{i}{2j}\right)b}{j-1} choices for S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} within these columns, as well as g⋅gcd⁡(i,j)≥gg\cdot\gcd(i,j)\geq g choices for the frame. Thus there are at least a positive constant times g​bj−1​ci−1gb^{j-1}c^{i-1} tight gradings obtained via this construction. ∎

The proof of Lemma 6.3 yields an explicit lower bound on the coefficient of g​bj−1​ci−1gb^{j-1}c^{i-1} in τ⁡(i,j)\tau(i,j). Instead of choosing S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} among the top c2\frac{c}{2} vertical edges, we can introduce a parameter λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1) and choose S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} from among the top λ​c\lambda c vertical edges. on the coefficient of g​bj−1​ci−1gb^{j-1}c^{i-1}.

Proof of Theorem 1.2(3).

Combining Lemma 6.3 and (6.2), we can confirm that

degb⁡τ⁡(k​d,k​e,1)=k​e−1​ and ​degc⁡τ⁡(k​d,k​e,1)=k​d−1.\deg_{b}\tau(kd,ke;1)=ke-1\text{ and }\deg_{c}\tau(kd,ke;1)=kd-1\,.

Then focusing on the top-degree term of each factor τ⁡(q​d,q​e,1)\tau(qd,qe;1) in part (4) of Theorem 1.2, we can see that the top-degree term of τ⁡(k​d,k​e,n)\tau(kd,ke;n) is a positive constant times bk​e−n​ck​d−nb^{ke-n}c^{kd-n}. ∎
