7. Weyl group symmetry

In this section, using tight gradings, we give a bijective proof of the Weyl group symmetry for cluster scattering diagrams, namely

(7.1) τb,c​(i,j)=τb,c​(i,b​i−j)​ and ​τb,c​(i,j)=τb,c​(c​j−i,j).\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{b,c}(i,bi-j)\text{ and }\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{b,c}(cj-i,j)\,.

This resolves Problem 1.1 posed by Elgin, Reading, and Stella [7].

7.1. Mutation and Retraction

One of the main tools we use is the Lee–Li–Zelevinsky mutation map [17]. Combining this mutation map with a new “retraction” map yields a bijection between collections of tight gradings that exhibit the Weyl group symmetries.

We start by recalling some of the notions from [17].

The remote shadow of S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}}, denoted by rsh⁡(S𝐍)\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}}), is the subset of sh⁡(S𝐍)\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) obtained by removing all horizontal edges of height s−1s-1 whenever vs∈S𝐍v_{s}\in S_{\mathbf{N}}. We say that e∈𝒫e\in\mathcal{P} is directly shadowed by e′∈𝒫e^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P} if e∈sh⁡(e′)e\in\sh(e^{\prime}) and sh⁡(e′)\sh(e^{\prime}) is minimal with respect to this property. Note that this is well defined because any pair of shadows are either disjoint or nested. For 0≤h<d20\leq h<d_{2} and 0<s≤d20<s\leq d_{2}, let rsh⁡(S𝐍)h;s\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}})_{h;s} denote the set of edges in rsh⁡(S𝐍)\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) of height hh that are directly shadowed by vsv_{s}. For 0<r≤|rsh⁡(S𝐍)h;s|0<r\leq|\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}})_{h;s}| let rsh⁡(S𝐍)h;s;r\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}})_{h;s;r} denote the rthr^{\text{th}} element of rsh⁡(S𝐍)h;s\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}})_{h;s}, ordered left-to-right.

Since a grading ω∈CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)\omega\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) is completely determined by the edge sets S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} and S𝐍S_{\mathbf{N}} where ω\omega is nonzero, from now on we identify such ω\omega with the pair (S𝐄,S𝐍)(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}}). This is precisely the setting of compatible pairs in [17]; see also the discussion below Definition 4.5.

Definition 7.2 ([17, Lemma 3.5]).

The mutation map

θ:CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)→CGb,c​(b​d2−d1,d2)\theta:\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j)\to\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(bd_{2}-d_{1},d_{2})

is defined for compatible gradings follows. Fix (S𝐄,S𝐍)∈CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}})\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j). Then we have θ⁡(S𝐄,S𝐍)=(S𝐄′,S𝐍′)\theta(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}})=(S_{\mathbf{E}}^{\prime},S_{\mathbf{N}}^{\prime}), where

S𝐍′={vs′:vd2+1−s∈𝒫2∖S𝐍}, and S_{\mathbf{N}}^{\prime}=\{v_{s}^{\prime}\,:\,v_{d_{2}+1-s}\in\mathcal{P}_{2}\setminus S_{\mathbf{N}}\},\text{ and }
S𝐄′={rsh⁡(S𝐍′)d2−s;d2−h;r:rsh⁡(S𝐍)h;s;r∈S𝐄}.S_{\mathbf{E}}^{\prime}=\{\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}}^{\prime})_{d_{2}-s;d_{2}-h;r}:\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}})_{h;s;r}\in S_{\mathbf{E}}\}.

The fact that the image of θ\theta consists of compatible gradings follows from [17, Lemmas 3.5 and 3.12]. Note that θ\theta forgets the information of the edges in 𝒫1​∖⁡sh⁡(S𝐍)\mathcal{P}_{1}\cut\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}).

Remark 7.3.

Our definition of the Lee–Li–Zelevinsky map θ\theta differs from their original formulation in [17]. We apply θ\theta to compatible gradings, rather than sets of vertical edges. It is straightforward to show that the two definitions are equivalent up to specifying a choice of horizontal edges. Note that we use the notation d1d_{1}, d2d_{2} in place of their parameters a1a_{1}, a2a_{2}.

In the definition of tight gradings, we have the condition that b​i​d2−c​j​d1=±gcd⁡(b​i,c​j)bid_{2}-cjd_{1}=\pm\gcd(bi,cj). The choice of sign determines the shadow structure of the tight grading, namely that S𝐄⊆sh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}}) when b​i​d2−c​j​d1=gcd⁡(b​i,c​j)bid_{2}-cjd_{1}=\gcd(bi,cj) and S𝐍⊆sh⁡(S𝐄)S_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}}) otherwise. We thus consider the following sets of shadowed gradings

CGb,c⊤​(d1,d2,i,j)\displaystyle\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) ≔{ω∈CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j):S𝐄⊆sh⁡(S𝐍)}, and\displaystyle\coloneqq\{\omega\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j):S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{N}})\}\,,\text{ and }
CGb,c⊢​(d1,d2,i,j)\displaystyle\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\vdash}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j) ≔{ω∈CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j):S𝐍⊆sh⁡(S𝐄)}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\{\omega\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j):S_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}})\}\,.
Proposition 7.4.

The mutation map θ\theta from 7.2 is injective when restricted to the set CGb,c⊤​(d1,d2,i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j).

Proof.

When (S𝐄,S𝐍)∈CGb,c⊤​(d1,d2,i,j)(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}})\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j), then we have S𝐄⊆rsh⁡(S𝐍)S_{\mathbf{E}}\subseteq\rsh(S_{\mathbf{N}}). Thus all the information about S𝐄S_{\mathbf{E}} is preserved under mutation. ∎

In addition to mutation, we require a retraction map for compatible gradings that forgets some of the vertical edges, namely those outside the shadow of the horizontal edges. This allows us to obtain shadowed gradings from compatible gradings, which will then enable us to get a tight grading in CGb,c⊢\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\vdash} from one in CGb,c⊤\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}.

Definition 7.5.

The retraction map

ϱ:CGb,c​(d1,d2,i,j)→∐0≤k≤iCGb,c⊢​(d1,d2,k,j)\varrho:\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j)\to\coprod_{0\leq k\leq i}\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\vdash}(d_{1},d_{2},k,j)

maps a compatible grading (S𝐄,S𝐍)(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}}) to (S𝐄,S𝐍∩sh⁡(S𝐄))(S_{\mathbf{E}},S_{\mathbf{N}}\cap\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}})).

7.2. Preservation on Tight Gradings

We now show that the Weyl group symmetry τb,c​(i,j)=τb,c​(c​j−i,j)\tau^{b,c}(i,j)=\tau^{b,c}(cj-i,j) is exhibited by the map ϱ∘θ\varrho\circ\theta, i.e., the composition of mutation and retraction, on the domain CGb,c⊤​(d1,d2,i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j). The other symmetry can be obtained by an analogous map, swapping the roles of vertical and horizontal edges.

Example 7.6.

Let b=3b=3, c=2c=2, (d1,d2,i,j)=(7,5,2,2)(d_{1},d_{2},i,j)=(7,5,2,2). Then ϱ∘θ\varrho\circ\theta acts on a particular tight grading as shown in Figure 6.

Let ω~\widetilde{\omega} be the grading obtained by applying the mutation map θ\theta post-composed by the retraction ϱ\varrho to ω∈CGb,c⊤​(d1,d2,i,j)\omega\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(d_{1},d_{2},i,j). Let S~𝐄\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}} and S~𝐍\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{N}} be the horizontal and vertical edges of nonzero weight in ω~\widetilde{\omega}, respectively.

Lemma 7.7.

We have ω~∈CGb,c⊢​(b​d2−d1,d2,c​j−i,j)\widetilde{\omega}\in\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\vdash}(bd_{2}-d_{1},d_{2},cj-i,j).

Proof.

By the definition of the retraction map, we can readily see that S~𝐍⊆sh⁡(S~𝐄)\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{N}}\subseteq\sh(\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}}). Moreover, since retraction only shrinks the set of vertical edges with nonzero grading value, then the compatibility of ω~\widetilde{\omega} follows directly from that of θ⁡(ω)\theta(\omega), shown in Proposition 7.4. Thus, it only remains to check the sizes of S~𝐄\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}} and S~𝐍\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{N}}.

By construction, we have |S~𝐄|=|S𝐄|=j\big|\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}}\big|=\big|S_{\mathbf{E}}\big|=j. Following from [17, Lemma 3.5], the edges in sh⁡(S~𝐄)⊇S~𝐍\sh(\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}})\supseteq\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{N}} correspond to {vmax}∪sh⁡(S𝐄)​∖​{vmin}\{v_{\max}\}\cup\sh(S_{\mathbf{E}})\cut\{v_{\min}\}. Since ω⁡(vm​i​n)=0\omega(v_{min})=0 by Lemma 4.13, the number of edges in S~𝐍\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{N}} is precisely |sh⁡(S~𝐄)|−i=c​j−i\big|\sh(\widetilde{S}_{\mathbf{E}})\big|-i=cj-i. ∎

Proof of Theorem 1.6.

It follows from Lemma 7.7 and the fact that

b⁡(c​j−i)​d2−c​j​(b​d2−d1)=c​j​d1−b​i​d2=−gcd⁡(b​i,c​j)b(cj-i)d_{2}-cj(bd_{2}-d_{1})=cjd_{1}-bid_{2}=-\gcd(bi,cj)

that ω~\widetilde{\omega} is also a tight grading. To see that this map is bijective, we first note that injectivity of θ\theta follows from Proposition 7.4, hence the injectivity of ρ∘θ\rho\circ\theta then follows Lemma 4.13. By applying the analogous map to the tight gradings in CGb,c⊤​(b​d2−d1,d2,c​j−i,j)\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top}(bd_{2}-d_{1},d_{2},cj-i,j), we obtain bijectivity. ∎

Remark 7.8.

The central wall ℝ≤0​(3,2)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(3,2) in 𝔇(3,2)\mathfrak{D}_{(3,2)} is preserved under the Weyl symmetry. Hence, this shows that the composition of mutation and retraction gives a bijection between the sets of tight gradings in CG3,2⊤⁡(3​i+2,2​i+1,i,i)\CG_{3,2}^{\top}(3i+2,2i+1,i,i) and in CG3,2⊢⁡(3​i+1,2​i+1,i,i)\CG_{3,2}^{\vdash}(3i+1,2i+1,i,i), each corresponding to coefficients of the central wall-function in 𝔇(3,2)\mathfrak{D}_{(3,2)}.

8. Counting tight gradings

Recall from the statement of Theorem 4.10(2) that for partitions 𝐏1⊢p\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash p and 𝐏2⊢q\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash q, λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) equals the number of tight gradings ω\omega on 𝒫⁡(d1,d2)\mathcal{P}(d_{1},d_{2}) with 𝐏1=(ω⁡(v)∣v∈S𝐍​(ω))\mathbf{P}_{1}=(\omega(v)\mid v\in S_{\mathbf{N}}(\omega)) and 𝐏2=(ω⁡(u)∣u∈S𝐄​(ω)),\mathbf{P}_{2}=(\omega(u)\mid u\in S_{\mathbf{E}}(\omega)), as long as d1≥pd_{1}\geq p and d2≥qd_{2}\geq q are chosen so that |p​d2−q​d1|=gcd⁡(p,q)|pd_{2}-qd_{1}|=\gcd(p,q). Nonetheless, determining λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) by counting tight gradings in general seems to be a very hard combinatorial problem. We first give a closed formula for λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) in the case where one of the partitions is of length one, which generalizes Corollary 4.16. Then we derive a total count of tight gradings with |𝐏1|=|𝐏2|=k|\mathbf{P}_{1}|=|\mathbf{P}_{2}|=k. Both proofs make use, in a sense, of wall-crossing formulas, namely, the additional information that the counts are encoded in consistent scattering diagrams. We conclude this section with a combinatorial argument in a special case.

For a partition 𝐏\mathbf{P}, write μ⁡(𝐏)\mu(\mathbf{P}) for its tuple of multiplicities and denote

(zμ⁡(𝐏))=z(z−1)⋯(z−ℓ(𝐏)+1)∏m∈μ⁡(𝐏)m!.\binom{z}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}=\dfrac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-\ell(\mathbf{P})+1)}{\prod\limits_{m\in\mu(\mathbf{P})}m!}.
Proposition 8.1.

For any 𝐏⊢j\mathbf{P}\vdash j, we have

(8.2) λ⁡((i),𝐏)=gcd⁡(i,j)i​(iμ⁡(𝐏)).\lambda((i),\mathbf{P})=\frac{\gcd(i,j)}{i}\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}.
Proof.

Consider the scattering diagrams 𝔇⁡(1+xi,P2)\mathfrak{D}(1+x^{i},P_{2}) and 𝔇⁡(1+x,P2i)\mathfrak{D}(1+x,P_{2}^{i}), where P2=1+∑k≥1p2,k​ykP_{2}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}p_{2,k}y^{k}. Note that we have the expansion

P2i=1+∑k≥1∑𝐐⊢k(iμ⁡(𝐐))​p2𝐐​yk,P_{2}^{i}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\vdash k}\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{Q})}p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}}y^{k},

where p2𝐐p_{2}^{\mathbf{Q}} denotes the monomial ∏k∈𝐐p2,k\prod_{k\in\mathbf{Q}}p_{2,k}.

The two scattering diagrams are related by a change-of-lattice transformation (slightly more general than Proposition 2.5 but can be proven similarly): the wall-function 𝔣⁡(xi​yj)\mathfrak{f}(x^{i}y^{j}) on ℝ≤0​(i,j)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(i,j) of 𝔇⁡(1+xi,P2)\mathfrak{D}(1+x^{i},P_{2}) and the wall-function 𝔣′​(x​yj)\mathfrak{f}^{\prime}(xy^{j}) on ℝ≤0​(1,j)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(1,j) of 𝔇⁡(1+x,P2i)\mathfrak{D}(1+x,P_{2}^{i}) are related by

𝔣⁡(x​yj)=𝔣′​(x​yj)gcd⁡(i,j)i.\mathfrak{f}(xy^{j})=\mathfrak{f}^{\prime}(xy^{j})^{\frac{\gcd(i,j)}{i}}.

Comparing the x​yjxy^{j}-coefficients on both sides yields

∑𝐏⊢jλ⁡((i),𝐏)​p2𝐏=gcd⁡(i,j)i​∑𝐐⊢jλ⁡((1),𝐐)​∏p∈𝐐∑𝐏⊢p(iμ⁡(𝐏))​p2𝐏.\sum_{\mathbf{P}\vdash j}\lambda((i),\mathbf{P})p_{2}^{\mathbf{P}}=\frac{\gcd(i,j)}{i}\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\vdash j}\lambda((1),\mathbf{Q})\prod_{p\in\mathbf{Q}}\sum_{\mathbf{P}\vdash p}\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}p_{2}^{\mathbf{P}}.

However, for any partition 𝐐\mathbf{Q} with ℓ⁡(𝐐)>1\ell(\mathbf{Q})>1, λ⁡((1),𝐐)=0\lambda((1),\mathbf{Q})=0 by its tight grading interpretation. As a special case of Corollary 4.16, we have λ⁡((1),(j))=1\lambda((1),(j))=1. Then the above equality reduces to

∑𝐏⊢jλ⁡((i),𝐏)​p2𝐏=gcd⁡(i,j)i​∑𝐏⊢j(iμ⁡(𝐏))​p2𝐏.\sum_{\mathbf{P}\vdash j}\lambda((i),\mathbf{P})p_{2}^{\mathbf{P}}=\frac{\gcd(i,j)}{i}\sum_{\mathbf{P}\vdash j}\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}p_{2}^{\mathbf{P}}.

The desired formula follows from comparing the p2𝐏p_{2}^{\mathbf{P}}-coefficients of each 𝐏\mathbf{P} on both sides. ∎

For example, if ℓ⁡(𝐏)>i\ell(\mathbf{P})>i, then λ⁡((i),𝐏)\lambda((i),\mathbf{P}) vanishes; if ℓ⁡(𝐏)=1\ell(\mathbf{P})=1, then λ⁡((i),(j))=gcd⁡(i,j)\lambda((i),(j))=\gcd(i,j). It is yet unclear how to show the formula (8.2) purely by tight grading combinatorics. One may allude to the analysis in the proof of Corollary 4.16, but notice that in general gcd⁡(i,j)\gcd(i,j) does not necessarily divide λ⁡((i),𝐏)\lambda((i),\mathbf{P}). See the end of this section for an example of tight grading combinatorics when ℓ⁡(𝐏)=i\ell(\mathbf{P})=i.

Further, we can derive one total count of tight gradings using the quiver methods of Section 3. We consider tight gradings of total weights (k,k)(k,k) on the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(k+1,k)\mathcal{P}(k+1,k) for k≥1k\geq 1, which proceeds from (0,0)(0,0) to (k+1,k)(k+1,k) in steps

E​(E​N)k=u1​u2​v1​u3​v2​…​uk+1​vk,E(EN)^{k}=u_{1}u_{2}v_{1}u_{3}v_{2}\ldots u_{k+1}v_{k},

where EE (resp. NN) denotes an east (resp. north) step. Our aim is to prove that they are counted by the series [20, A002293]:

Proposition 8.3.

The number of tight gradings of total weights (k,k)(k,k) on 𝒫⁡(k+1,k)\mathcal{P}(k+1,k) equals

∑𝐏1⊢k∑𝐏2⊢kλ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)=14​k+1​(4​k+1k)=13​k+1​(4​kk).\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash k}\sum_{\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash k}\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})=\frac{1}{4k+1}\binom{4k+1}{k}=\frac{1}{3k+1}\binom{4k}{k}.
Proof.

Let ℓ1\ell_{1}, ℓ2\ell_{2} be arbitrary positive integers. We consider the tropical vertex as in [4, Section 3], with variables pi,jp_{i,j} specialized to

pi,j=(ℓij),i=1,2,j≥1.p_{i,j}=\binom{\ell_{i}}{j},\;i=1,2,\,j\geq 1.

Then [4, Theorem 3.5] (see also Theorem 4.10) reads as follows:

f(1,1)=1+∑k≥1∑ωwt⁡(ω)​(x​y)k,f_{(1,1)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\sum_{\omega}{\rm wt}(\omega)(xy)^{k},

where the inner sum ranges over all tight gradings ω\omega on 𝒫⁡(k+1,k)\mathcal{P}(k+1,k) as above, and the weight is defined as

wt⁡(ω)=∏i=1k+1(ℓ1ω⁡(ui))​∏j=1k(ℓ2ω⁡(vj)).{\rm wt}(\omega)=\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}\binom{\ell_{1}}{\omega(u_{i})}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\binom{\ell_{2}}{\omega(v_{j})}.

On the other hand, we consider again the refined GW/Kronecker correspondence [23]. Namely, vanishing results for Euler characteristic of quiver moduli yield by [23, Section 11]:

f(1,1)=H​(x​y)ℓ1​ℓ2,f_{(1,1)}=H(xy)^{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}},

where the series H⁡(z)H(z) is determined by the functional equation

H⁡(z)=(1−z​H​(z)ℓ1​ℓ2−ℓ1−ℓ2)−1.H(z)=(1-zH(z)^{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}-\ell_{1}-\ell_{2}})^{-1}.

Applying the Lagrange inversion formula (similarly to [23, Corollary 11.2]) we find

f(1,1)=1+∑k≥1ℓ1​ℓ2(ℓ1−1)​(ℓ2−1)​k+ℓ1​ℓ2​((ℓ1−1)​(ℓ2−1)​k+ℓ1​ℓ2k)​(x​y)k.f_{(1,1)}=1+\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}{(\ell_{1}-1)(\ell_{2}-1)k+\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\binom{(\ell_{1}-1)(\ell_{2}-1)k+\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}{k}(xy)^{k}.

Comparing coefficients, we find

∑ω∏i=1k+1(ℓ1ω⁡(ui))​∏j=1k(ℓ2ω⁡(vj))=ℓ1​ℓ2(ℓ1−1)​(ℓ2−1)​k+ℓ1​ℓ2​((ℓ1−1)​(ℓ2−1)​k+ℓ1​ℓ2k).\sum_{\omega}\prod_{i=1}^{k+1}\binom{\ell_{1}}{\omega(u_{i})}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\binom{\ell_{2}}{\omega(v_{j})}=\frac{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}{(\ell_{1}-1)(\ell_{2}-1)k+\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\binom{{(\ell_{1}-1)(\ell_{2}-1)k+\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}}{k}.

We note that both sides behave polynomially in ℓ1\ell_{1}, ℓ2\ell_{2}. Since the identity holds for all nonnegative ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2}, it holds as an identity of (degree kk) polynomials in ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2}, considered as variables. We can therefore specialize ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2} to −1-1. Using

(−1k)=(−1)k,\binom{-1}{k}=(-1)^{k},

we find

∑ω(−1)k​(−1)k=14​k+1​(4​k+1k).\sum_{\omega}(-1)^{k}(-1)^{k}=\frac{1}{4k+1}\binom{4k+1}{k}.

But the left-hand side is just the number of all tight gradings on 𝒫⁡(k+1,k)\mathcal{P}(k+1,k), finishing the proof.∎

Finally, to give a better sense concerning the combinatorics of tight gradings, we close this section with a second proof of Proposition 8.1 restricted to the special case that i=ji=j.

Combinatorial Proof of Proposition 8.1 when i=ji=j.

When 𝐏⊢i\mathbf{P}\vdash i, we have λ⁡((i),𝐏)=(iμ⁡(𝐏))\lambda((i),\mathbf{P})=\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}, which can be rewritten as

(iμ⁡(𝐏))=i(i−1)⋯(i−ℓ(𝐏)+1)∏m∈μ⁡(𝐏)m!=i!∏m∈μ⁡(𝐏¯)m!\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})}=\frac{i(i-1)\cdots(i-\ell(\mathbf{P})+1)}{\prod_{m\in\mu(\mathbf{P})}m!}=\frac{i!}{\prod_{m\in\mu(\overline{\mathbf{P}})}m!}

where 𝐏¯\overline{\mathbf{P}} is the partition 𝐏\mathbf{P} extended to length ii by appending (i−ℓ)(i-\ell) zeroes. Consequently, λ⁡((i),𝐏)=(iμ⁡(𝐏))\lambda((i),\mathbf{P})=\binom{i}{\mu(\mathbf{P})} counts the number of rearrangements of the extended partition 𝐏¯\overline{\mathbf{P}} of length ii (including zeroes).

We demonstrate the following bijection between the set of tight gradings on 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i) with 𝐏1=(i)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(i) and 𝐏2⊢i\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash i and the set of rearrangements of 𝐏2¯\overline{\mathbf{P}_{2}}:

1) The Maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i) has the form E​(E​N)iE(EN)^{i}. Given the composition (a1,a2,…,ai)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{i}) which is a rearrangement of 𝐏2¯\overline{\mathbf{P}_{2}}, such that 0≤aj≤i0\leq a_{j}\leq i and a1+a2+⋯+ai=ia_{1}+a_{2}+\dots+a_{i}=i, we show there is a unique tight grading with ω2​(vj)=aj\omega_{2}(v_{j})=a_{j} where vjv_{j} is the jjth NN step of 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i).

2) We claim by use of the Cycle Lemma [6], there is a unique choice of 0≤h≤i−10\leq h\leq i-1 such that we have the following inequalities satisfied by partial sums:

For​1≤g≤h,∑m=1−h+ig−h+iam≤(g−1),and​for​h<g≤i,(∑m=1−h+iiam+∑m=1g−ham)≤g.\mathrm{For~}1\leq g\leq h,~~\sum_{m=1-h+i}^{g-h+i}a_{m}\leq(g-1),~~~\mathrm{and~for~}h<g\leq i,~~\left(\sum_{m=1-h+i}^{i}a_{m}+\sum_{m=1}^{g-h}a_{m}\right)\leq g.

To see this, we first extend the composition (a1,a2,…,ai)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{i}) to one of length i+1i+1 by assigning a0=0a_{0}=0, and then turn (a0,a1,a2,…,ai)(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{i}) into a lattice path from (0,0)(0,0) to (i+1,i)(i+1,i) of the form E(Na0)E(Na1)E(Na2)⋯E(Nai)E(N^{a_{0}})E(N^{a_{1}})E(N^{a_{2}})\cdots E(N^{a_{i}}), i.e. for 0≤g≤i0\leq g\leq i, alternate between a single EE step and a sequence of aga_{g} NN steps. Since a0+a1+a2+⋯+ai=ia_{0}+a_{1}+a_{2}+\dots+a_{i}=i, we reach (i+1,i)(i+1,i) as desired. The Cycle Lemma states that there is a unique cyclic rotation of the steps of this lattice path that yields a Dyck path. That rotation yielding the Dyck path equivalently yields a rotated tuple (aj,aj+1,…,ai−1,ai,a0,a1,a2,…,aj−1)(a_{j},a_{j+1},\dots,a_{i-1},a_{i},a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{j-1}) satisfying the system of inequalities aj≤0a_{j}\leq 0, aj+aj+1≤1a_{j}+a_{j+1}\leq 1, aj+aj+1+aj+2≤2a_{j}+a_{j+1}+a_{j+2}\leq 2, and continuing so that each length gg partial sum is less or equal to g−1g-1. Removing the entry for a0=0a_{0}=0, we obtain the above system of inequalities after letting j=i+1−hj=i+1-h.

3) The points closest to the diagonal of 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i) are p0=(0,0)p_{0}=(0,0), p1=(i,i−1),p2=(i−1,i−2),…,pi−1=(2,1)p_{1}=(i,i-1),p_{2}=(i-1,i-2),\dots,p_{i-1}=(2,1). Starting with a composition (a1,a2,…,ai)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{i}) as above, we identify the unique choice of hh (in the range 0≤h≤i−10\leq h\leq i-1) such that the above system of inequalities is satisfied. Then we work in the frame starting at point php_{h} but for 1≤j≤i1\leq j\leq i, let ω2​(vj)=aj\omega_{2}(v_{j})=a_{j} where vjv_{j} is the jjth NN step of 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i), so that v1v_{1} is the NN step after the unique E​EEE subsequence of 𝒫⁡(i+1,i)\mathcal{P}(i+1,i). If ℓ⁡(𝐏2)=ρ\ell(\mathbf{P}_{2})=\rho, we get ρ⁡(ρ+1)/2\rho(\rho+1)/2 tiles as part of the horizontal footprint attached to these vertical edges.

By construction of this tight grading, starting the frame from php_{h}, this means we have tiles of length ai+1−ha_{i+1-h} in the bottom row, length ai+1−h+ai+2−ha_{i+1-h}+a_{i+2-h} in the row 22nd from the bottom, and continuing so we have tiles of length ai+1−h+ai+2−h+⋯+ai+j−ha_{i+1-h}+a_{i+2-h}+\dots+a_{i+j-h} in the row jjth from the bottom, and length a1+a2+⋯+ai=ia_{1}+a_{2}+\dots+a_{i}=i on the top row.

By the corresponding system of inequalities for this choice of hh, we have exactly enough room for the vertical tile of length ii corresponding to partition 𝐏1=(i)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(i) on the leftmost horizontal edge of this frame. ∎

We illustrate this proof with Example 8.4.

Example 8.4.

Suppose that 𝐏1=(i)=(3)\mathbf{P}_{1}=(i)=(3) and 𝐏2⊢3\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash 3. We work with the maximal Dyck path 𝒫⁡(4,3)\mathcal{P}(4,3) of the form E​E​N​E​N​E​NEENENEN. If 𝐏2=(3)\mathbf{P}_{2}=(3), 𝐏2¯=(3,0,0)\overline{\mathbf{P}_{2}}=(3,0,0) and the possible rearrangements are (a1,a2,a3)=(0,0,3),(0,3,0)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})=(0,0,3),(0,3,0), or (3,0,0)(3,0,0). The corresponding tight gradings are illustrated, respectively, in the top row of Figure 7. The arrangement of these tight gradings in Figure 7 was also chosen so that relative to the use of the Cycle Lemma in Step 2, h=0h=0 for the tight gradings (and corresponding 33-tuples (a1,a2,a3)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})) in the leftmost column, h=1h=1 for those in the middle column, and h=2h=2 for those in the rightmost column. 9. Final remarks

9.1. Combinatorics of tight gradings

In Section 5, we described a process for generating a tiling associated to each tight grading. This tiling is only a partial tiling, in that there can be empty spaces in the region between the Dyck path and the frame. It could be interesting to characterize the number of such spaces, and in particular study the case of “tightest gradings” when no such spaces appear. Note that this tiling construction is different from that described in [4] and [5], in that the footprints contain a superset of the tiles in earlier constructions.

As discussed in Remark 7.8, the composition of mutation and retractions gives a bijection between the tight gradings in CG3,2⊤⁡(3​i+2,2​i+1,i,i)\CG_{3,2}^{\top}(3i+2,2i+1,i,i) and in CG3,2⊢⁡(3​i+1,2​i+1,i,i)\CG_{3,2}^{\vdash}(3i+1,2i+1,i,i). Each set of tight gradings gives a combinatorial interpretation of τ3,2​(i,i)\tau^{3,2}(i,i). The two sets of tight gradings correspond to a choice of positive or negative angular momentum broken line in the scattering diagram 𝔇(3,2)\mathfrak{D}_{(3,2)}, as described in [5]. It would be interesting to construct a general bijection between the sets of tight gradings in CGb,c⊢\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\vdash} and CGb,c⊤\mathrm{CG}_{\mathit{b},\mathit{c}}^{\top} that each give a combinatorial interpretation to the same wall-function coefficient.

9.2. Potential relation with stable trees

There are several situations where Euler characteristics of quiver moduli spaces can be computed by counting so-called stable trees [26]. In fact, this is one of the main techniques in [23] for obtaining the formulas which are used in Section 3. It is thus natural to ask for bijections between sets of stable trees and sets of tight gradings (maybe suitably weighted), but no general pattern emerged yet. One obstacle for such constructions is the fact that the notion of tight gradings is well-adapted to the natural Weyl group symmetry, whereas stable trees are not (the Weyl group symmetry corresponds to applying reflection functors to quiver representations, which does not preserve the class of tree representations naturally).

9.3. Algebraicity and growth rate

The conjectural wall-function in C13 has the first few terms

1+2​x12​x25+5​x14​x210+17​x16​x215+64​x18​x220+259​x110​x225+⋯.1+2x_{1}^{2}x_{2}^{5}+5x_{1}^{4}x_{2}^{10}+17x_{1}^{6}x_{2}^{15}+64x_{1}^{8}x_{2}^{20}+259x_{1}^{10}x_{2}^{25}+\cdots.

Write the generating function as

S⁡(x)=1+2​x+5​x2+17​x3+⋯.S(x)=1+2x+5x^{2}+17x^{3}+\cdots.

Let A⁡(x)=1−x​S​(x)A(x)=1-xS(x). According to [20, A217596], it satisfies the algebraic equation

A​(x)3=A​(x)2−x​A​(x)−x2.A(x)^{3}=A(x)^{2}-xA(x)-x^{2}.

Then it follows that the coefficients have asymptotic exponential growth rate 27/527/5.

Notice that according to the proof of Proposition 3.5, the wall-function on ℝ≤0​(b,c)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(b,c) is algebraic over ℚ⁡(x1i​b​x2j​c)\mathbb{Q}(x_{1}^{ib}x_{2}^{jc}). The coefficients have asymptotic growth rate mm(m−1)m−1\frac{m^{m}}{(m-1)^{m-1}} where m=(b−1)​(c−1)m=(b-1)(c-1), assuming b,c>1b,c>1.

It is an interesting question whether every wall-function 𝔣ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)\mathfrak{f}_{\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec)} with of a cluster scattering diagram is algebraic (first asked by Kontsevich [12, Section 1.4]) and whether the coefficients asymptotically always have an exponential growth rate when b​c>4bc>4 and ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec) is in the “Badlands”, i.e.,

(9.1) ed∈(b​c−b​c​(b​c−4)2​c,b​c+b​c​(b​c−4)2​c).\frac{e}{d}\in\left(\frac{bc-\sqrt{bc(bc-4)}}{2c},\frac{bc+\sqrt{bc(bc-4)}}{2c}\right).

Based on numerical experiments, we propose the following conjecture.

Conjecture 9.2.

For any rr in the open interval (9.1), the limit

f⁡(r)≔limji→r,i→∞ln⁡τ⁡(i,j)b​c​i​j−b​i2−c​j2f(r)\coloneqq\lim_{\frac{j}{i}\to r,\,i\to\infty}\frac{\ln\tau(i,j)}{\sqrt{bcij-bi^{2}-cj^{2}}}

exists and is continuous in rr.

By taking r=e/dr=e/d and the sequence (i,j)=(k​d,k​e)(i,j)=(kd,ke) for k≥1k\geq 1, Conjecture 9.2 implies an exponential asymptotic growth of the coefficients along the wall ℝ≤0​(d​b,e​c)\mathbb{R}_{\leq 0}(db,ec). Using the Weyl group symmetry (7.1), one can further show that f⁡(r)f(r) is bounded provided continuity.

In the case where b=cb=c, Conjecture 9.2 implies a conjecture of Michael Douglas stated in [26, Conjecture 6.1] and [12, Section 6 (iii)], where τ⁡(d,e)\tau(d,e) equals the Euler characteristic χ⁡(Md,es​(b))\chi(M^{s}_{d,e}(b)) defined therein. We remark, however, unlike [26, Conjecture 6.1] that we do not expect f⁡(r)f(r) to extend continuously to the endpoints of the interval (9.1).

Appendix A Tables of λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2})

We present tables of λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) for 𝐏1⊢k\mathbf{P}_{1}\vdash k, 𝐏2⊢k\mathbf{P}_{2}\vdash k, 2≤k≤62\leq k\leq 6. Notice that for a given kk, the total sum of the entries is computed in Proposition 8.3. The formulas for the first row (equivalently the first column) of such tables are given by Proposition 8.1. Since |𝐏1|=|𝐏2||\mathbf{P}_{1}|=|\mathbf{P}_{2}|, the combinatorial argument at the end of Section 8 also applies. A formula for general λ⁡(𝐏1,𝐏2)\lambda(\mathbf{P}_{1},\mathbf{P}_{2}) is currently unknown.
